Autoregressive Language Models are Secretly Energy-Based Models:
Insights into the Lookahead Capabilities of Next-Token Prediction

Mathieu Blondel Affiliation: Google DeepMind    Michaël E. Sander Affiliation: Google DeepMind    Germain Vivier-Ardisson Affiliation: Google DeepMind    Tianlin Liu Affiliation: Google DeepMind    Vincent Roulet Correspondence to: mblondel@google.com Affiliation: Google DeepMind
Abstract

Autoregressive models (ARMs) currently constitute the dominant paradigm for large language models (LLMs). Energy-based models (EBMs) represent another class of models, which have historically been less prevalent in LLM development, yet naturally characterize the optimal policy in post-training alignment. In this paper, we present a unified view of these two model classes. Taking the chain rule of probability as a starting point, we establish an explicit bijection between ARMs and EBMs in function space, which we show to correspond to a special case of the soft Bellman equation in maximum entropy reinforcement learning. Building upon this bijection, we derive the equivalence between supervised learning of ARMs and EBMs. Furthermore, we analyze the distillation of EBMs into ARMs by providing theoretical error bounds. Our results provide insights into the ability of ARMs to plan ahead, despite being based on the next-token prediction paradigm.

Keywords: 
autoregressive models, energy-based model, maxent RL, dynamic programming

1 Introduction

Autoregressive models (ARMs), which are based on the next-token prediction paradigm, currently constitute the dominant approach for large language models (LLMs). Their primary advantages lie in their highly parallelizable training and the ability to perform exact ancestral sampling. Energy-based models (EBMs) represent another class of models, which inherently have the ability to look ahead, since they define sequence-level distributions. However, they have historically been less prevalent, since they require computing an intractable partition function over the set of all possible sequences. Consequently, they are significantly more challenging to train and sample from, often necessitating Markov-chain Monte-Carlo (MCMC) methods.

Following pre-training, LLMs typically undergo a post-training alignment phase. This process is frequently framed as maximum entropy (MaxEnt) reinforcement learning (RL), a.k.a. entropy-regularized RL, where we seek a probability distribution (or policy) that maximizes a trade-off between the expected reward and a Kullback-Leibler (KL) regularization term. Crucially, if we maximize over the set of all possible probability distributions, the analytical solution to this objective is exactly an EBM. Therefore, finding an ARM that maximizes this objective is equivalent to distilling an EBM into an ARM.

This perspective raises a fundamental question: To what extent can ARMs approximate EBMs? From a probabilistic graphical model standpoint, ARMs are Bayesian networks (directed graphical models), whereas EBMs are Markov random fields (undirected graphical models). However, ARMs rely on the chain rule of probability, which can, in principle, decompose any probability distribution. It naturally follows that ARMs should be convertible into EBMs, and vice-versa. Building upon these intuitions, we derive several results that provide insights into the approximation power of ARMs w.r.t. EBMs, and consequently their ability to plan ahead, despite being based on the next-token prediction paradigm.

Contributions.

  • •

    We provide a unified view of ARMs and EBMs, exhibiting clear structural analogies between these two model classes.

  • •

    In function space (a.k.a. tabular setting in RL), we establish an exact bijection between ARMs and EBMs (Proposition 3.2). While our starting point is the chain rule of probability, our bijection can be viewed as an instance of the soft Bellman equation in MaxEnt RL. Our result demonstrates that in our setting the soft Bellman equation naturally emerges as a direct consequence of the chain rule of probability.

  • •

    Building upon this bijection, we derive the equivalence between supervised learning of ARMs and EBMs (Proposition 4.1). Furthermore, we derive error bounds for distilling EBMs into ARMs (Proposition 4.2), a process identical to MaxEnt RL. Our results, validated through numerical experiments, provide some theoretical justification for the next-token prediction paradigm and for teacher forcing.

Notation.

Let VV be the vocabulary size, and let 𝒱≔{1,…,V}{\mathcal{V}}\coloneqq\{1,\ldots,V\} be the vocabulary set. We denote the set of sequences of size tt in the vocabulary by 𝒱t{\mathcal{V}}^{t}. We consider two special tokens that are excluded from 𝒱{\mathcal{V}}: a BOS (beginning of sequence) token that encodes the beginning of a prompt and a EOS (end of sequence) token that encodes the end of a response. We then denote the set of prompts of maximal size UU (BOS included) by 𝒳={BOS}×∪t=1U−1𝒱t{\mathcal{X}}=\{\texttt{BOS}\}\times\cup_{t=1}^{U-1}{\mathcal{V}}^{t}, and the set of responses of maximal size TT (EOS included) by 𝒴=∪t=1T−1𝒱t×{EOS}{\mathcal{Y}}=\cup_{t=1}^{T-1}{\mathcal{V}}^{t}\times\{\texttt{EOS}\}. 2 A unified perspective on EBMs and ARMs

2.1 Energy-based models (EBMs)

Model definition.

EBMs (Ackley et al., 1985; LeCun et al., 2007) use a function R:𝒳×𝒴→ℝR\colon{\mathcal{X}}\times{\mathcal{Y}}\to{\mathbb{R}}, measuring the “affinity” between an input 𝒙∈𝒳{\bm{x}}\in{\mathcal{X}} (a prompt) and an output 𝒚∈𝒴{\bm{y}}\in{\mathcal{Y}} (a complete response). We use the convention that higher value means higher affinity, therefore RR can be interpreted as a negative energy. EBMs are defined as

pRebm​(𝒚|𝒙)≔exp⁡(R⁡(𝒙,𝒚))∑𝒚′∈𝒴exp⁡(R⁡(𝒙,𝒚′)),p^{\textsc{ebm}}_{R}({\bm{y}}|{\bm{x}})\coloneqq\frac{\exp(R({\bm{x}},{\bm{y}}))}{\sum_{{\bm{y}}^{\prime}\in{\mathcal{Y}}}\exp(R({\bm{x}},{\bm{y}}^{\prime}))}, (1)

or more concisely, pRebm(⋅|𝒙)=softargmax(R(𝒙,⋅))p^{\textsc{ebm}}_{R}(\cdot|{\bm{x}})=\mathrm{softargmax}(R({\bm{x}},\cdot)). We use the letter RR on purpose, as it will coincide with the notion of reward function in RL. The reward could be a learned model or a given function, such as a verifier.

The associated sequence-level log-partition function is

ARebm(𝒙)≔LSE𝒚∈𝒴R(𝒙,𝒚)≔log∑𝒚∈𝒴exp(R(𝒙,𝒚)).A^{\textsc{ebm}}_{R}({\bm{x}})\coloneqq\underset{{\bm{y}}\in{\mathcal{Y}}}{{\mathrm{LSE}}}~R({\bm{x}},{\bm{y}})\coloneqq\log\sum_{{\bm{y}}\in{\mathcal{Y}}}\exp(R({\bm{x}},{\bm{y}})). (2)

We then have pRebm​(𝒚|𝒙)=exp⁡(R⁡(𝒙,𝒚)−ARebm​(𝒙))p^{\textsc{ebm}}_{R}({\bm{y}}|{\bm{x}})=\exp(R({\bm{x}},{\bm{y}})-A^{\textsc{ebm}}_{R}({\bm{x}})).

Unfortunately, the log-partition costs O⁡(VT)O(V^{T}) to compute exactly. This makes both learning EBMs and making inference with EBMs very challenging.

EBMs as undirected graphical models.

We can view EBMs as specifying a sequence-level Gibbs (Boltzmann) distribution parameterized by a function RR. From a probabilistic graphical model perspective, EBMs are (conditional) Markov random fields, that is, undirected graphical models.

Validity of the distribution.

Since all sequences 𝒚∈𝒴{\bm{y}}\in{\mathcal{Y}} have a maximal size TT, and therefore 𝒴{\mathcal{Y}} is finite, the denominator in (1) is well-defined. Exponentiation and renormalization ensure that it is a valid probability distribution.

Learning RR from data using Transformers. To learn RR from data, we must use a model that can cope with variable-length sequences 𝒙{\bm{x}} and 𝒚{\bm{y}}. This can be achieved using a Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017). Because RR is sequence-level, the Transformer can be non-causal (bidirectional). A Transformer embeds an input sequence 𝒔=𝒙⊕𝒚{\bm{s}}={\bm{x}}\oplus{\bm{y}} of size MM into a latent space ℝD{\mathbb{R}}^{D}, processing it through multiple attention, feedforward and normalization layers, yielding MM output vectors (𝒉1,…,𝒉M)({\bm{h}}_{1},\ldots,{\bm{h}}_{M}), where 𝒉i∈ℝD{\bm{h}}_{i}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{D}. When using a non-causal Transformer, each 𝒉i∈ℝD{\bm{h}}_{i}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{D} depends on the entire sequence 𝒔{\bm{s}}. To obtain a scalar-valued R⁡(𝒙,𝒚)R({\bm{x}},{\bm{y}}), one can for example use an affine layer on top of a single representation 𝒉¯\bar{\bm{h}} of the sequence. The latter can be the average of all 𝒉i{\bm{h}}_{i}, or simply the first vector 𝒉1{\bm{h}}_{1}, which mirrors the CLS token in BERT encoders (Devlin et al., 2019).

Learning RR from (𝒙,𝒚)({\bm{x}},{\bm{y}}) pairs is challenging due to the intractable normalization constant, and has attracted a large body of work (Song & Kingma, 2021; Sander et al., 2025). To work around this difficulty, RR is popularly learned from pairwise preferences (𝒙,𝒚+,𝒚−)({\bm{x}},{\bm{y}}^{+},{\bm{y}}^{-}), where 𝒚+{\bm{y}}^{+} is preferred over 𝒚−{\bm{y}}^{-} given 𝒙{\bm{x}} (Ziegler et al., 2019; Stiennon et al., 2020; Ouyang et al., 2022) or from scored pairs (𝒙,𝒚,s)({\bm{x}},{\bm{y}},s), where ss is the affinity score (binary or real valued) between 𝒙{\bm{x}} and 𝒚{\bm{y}}, that R⁡(𝒙,𝒚)R({\bm{x}},{\bm{y}}) should approximate (Cobbe et al., 2021).

Sampling.

Given RR, drawing i.i.d. sequence samples

Y∼pRebm(⋅|𝒙)Y\sim p^{\textsc{ebm}}_{R}(\cdot|{\bm{x}}) (3)

typically requires Markov-chain Monte-Carlo (MCMC) methods, such as Gibbs sampling. However, such samplers are typically inherently sequential and difficult to parallelize. Moreover, since they are never run to convergence in practice, they do not generate truly i.i.d. samples.

Optimal solution of MaxEnt RL as an EBM.

It is well-known that an EBM can be seen as the solution of

pRebm=argmaxp∈𝒫⁡(𝒴|𝒳)𝔼X𝔼Y∼p(⋅|X)R(X,Y)+H(p(⋅|X)),p^{\textsc{ebm}}_{R}=\argmax_{p\in{\mathcal{P}}({\mathcal{Y}}|{\mathcal{X}})}{\mathbb{E}}_{X}{\mathbb{E}}_{Y\sim p(\cdot|X)}R(X,Y)+H\big(p(\cdot|X)\big), (4)

where H⁡(⋅)H(\cdot) is the entropy of a distribution. More generally, RL-based post-training of LLMs is commonly formulated as the KL-regularized problem (Ziegler et al., 2019; Stiennon et al., 2020; Ouyang et al., 2022)

argmaxp∈𝒫⁡(𝒴|𝒳)𝔼X𝔼Y∼p(⋅|X)R(X,Y)−KL(p(⋅|X),pref(⋅|X)),\argmax_{p\in{\mathcal{P}}({\mathcal{Y}}|{\mathcal{X}})}{\mathbb{E}}_{X}{\mathbb{E}}_{Y\sim p(\cdot|X)}R(X,Y)-\mathrm{KL}(p(\cdot|X),p_{\mathrm{ref}}(\cdot|X)), (5)

where pref∈𝒫⁡(𝒴|𝒳)p_{\mathrm{ref}}\in{\mathcal{P}}({\mathcal{Y}}|{\mathcal{X}}) is a reference “anchor” distribution. The optimal solution p⋆p^{\star} is then

p⋆​(𝒚|𝒙)=pref​(𝒚|𝒙)​exp⁡(R⁡(𝒙,𝒚))∑𝒚′∈𝒴pref​(𝒚′|𝒙)​exp⁡(R⁡(𝒙,𝒚′)).p^{\star}({\bm{y}}|{\bm{x}})=\frac{p_{\mathrm{ref}}({\bm{y}}|{\bm{x}})\exp(R({\bm{x}},{\bm{y}}))}{\sum_{{\bm{y}}^{\prime}\in{\mathcal{Y}}}p_{\mathrm{ref}}({\bm{y}}^{\prime}|{\bm{x}})\exp(R({\bm{x}},{\bm{y}}^{\prime}))}. (6)

Using (1), we can write p⋆p^{\star} more concisely as p⋆=pR+Rrefebmp^{\star}=p^{\textsc{ebm}}_{R+R_{\mathrm{ref}}}, where Rref​(𝒙,𝒚)≔log⁡pref​(𝒚|𝒙)R_{\mathrm{ref}}({\bm{x}},{\bm{y}})\coloneqq\log p_{\mathrm{ref}}({\bm{y}}|{\bm{x}}). Therefore, the optimal solution of the KL-regularized RL objective (5) is exactly an EBM, with the reward function R+RrefR+R_{\mathrm{ref}}. Recently, several papers have replaced the KL divergence in the regularization term by other ff-divergences (Go et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024; Roulet et al., 2025; Sander et al., 2025).

2.2 Autoregressive models (ARMs)

Model definition.

Let us define the set of contexts 𝒮≔{BOS}×∪t=1U+T−2𝒱t{\mathcal{S}}\coloneqq\{\texttt{BOS}\}\times\cup_{t=1}^{U+T-2}{\mathcal{V}}^{t}. We can think of 𝒮{\mathcal{S}} as the set of partial (incomplete) sequences, including the initial prompt. Recall that we denoted 𝒜≔𝒱∪{EOS}{\mathcal{A}}\coloneqq{\mathcal{V}}\cup\{\texttt{EOS}\} the augmented vocabulary used to encode finished responses. Given a pair (𝒙,𝒚)({\bm{x}},{\bm{y}}), where 𝒚=(y1,…,yτ){\bm{y}}=(y_{1},\dots,y_{\tau}), it will be convenient to define the context (state) at time tt by

𝒔t≔𝒙⊕𝒚<t∈𝒮⁡(𝒙),{\bm{s}}_{t}\coloneqq{\bm{x}}\oplus{\bm{y}}_{<t}\\ \in{\mathcal{S}}({\bm{x}}), (7)

where 𝒮⁡(𝒙)⊆𝒮{\mathcal{S}}({\bm{x}})\subseteq{\mathcal{S}} is the set of partial sequences prolonging the prompt 𝒙{\bm{x}}. We assume that we have at our disposal a function q:𝒮×𝒜q\colon{\mathcal{S}}\times{\mathcal{A}}, for scoring the “affinity” between a context (state) 𝒔t∈𝒮{\bm{s}}_{t}\in{\mathcal{S}} and a next token yt∈𝒜y_{t}\in{\mathcal{A}} (potentially EOS). We can think of qq as a local scoring function, while RR used by EBMs is a global scoring function. ARMs (Bengio et al., 2003) use the chain rule of probability to define the probability of a sequence 𝒚{\bm{y}} given 𝒙{\bm{x}} as

pqarm​(𝒚|𝒙)≔∏t=1|𝒚|πq​(yt|𝒙⊕𝒚<t⏟𝒔t),p^{\textsc{arm}}_{q}({\bm{y}}|{\bm{x}})\coloneqq\prod_{t=1}^{|{\bm{y}}|}\pi_{q}(y_{t}|\underbrace{{\bm{x}}\oplus{\bm{y}}_{<t}}_{{\bm{s}}_{t}}), (8)

where

πq​(yt|𝒔t)≔exp⁡(q⁡(𝒔t,yt))∑j∈𝒜exp⁡(q⁡(𝒔t,j)).\pi_{q}(y_{t}|{\bm{s}}_{t})\coloneqq\frac{\exp(q({\bm{s}}_{t},y_{t}))}{\sum_{j\in{\mathcal{A}}}\exp(q({\bm{s}}_{t},j))}. (9)

The latter can be rewritten more concisely as πq(⋅|𝒔t)=softargmax(q(𝒔t,⋅))\pi_{q}(\cdot|{\bm{s}}_{t})=\mathrm{softargmax}(q({\bm{s}}_{t},\cdot)). The associated log-partition is

Vq(𝒔t)≔LSEj∈𝒜q(𝒔t,j)≔log∑j∈𝒜exp(q(𝒔t,j)).V_{q}({\bm{s}}_{t})\coloneqq\underset{j\in{\mathcal{A}}}{{\mathrm{LSE}}}~q({\bm{s}}_{t},j)\coloneqq\log\sum_{j\in{\mathcal{A}}}\exp(q({\bm{s}}_{t},j)). (10)

We then have πq​(yt|𝒔t)=exp⁡(q⁡(𝒔t,yt)−Vq​(𝒔t))\pi_{q}(y_{t}|{\bm{s}}_{t})=\exp(q({\bm{s}}_{t},y_{t})-V_{q}({\bm{s}}_{t})).

ARMs as directed graphical models.

From a probabilistic graphical model perspective, ARMs are Bayesian networks, that is, directed graphical models. More specifically, we can view ARMs as specifying a time-inhomogeneous infinite-order Markov chain (assuming unlimited context window size) with discrete states YtY_{t}.

Validity of the distribution.

For pqarm(⋅|𝒙)p^{\textsc{arm}}_{q}(\cdot|{\bm{x}}) to define a valid probability distribution over all possible sequences of size at most TT, we need to enforce that sequences cannot be of size more than TT. This can be achieved by fixing

q⁡(𝒔T,yT)≔{0if​yT=EOS−∞if​yT≠EOS.q({\bm{s}}_{T},y_{T})\coloneqq\begin{cases}0&\mbox{if}~y_{T}=\texttt{EOS}\\ -\infty&\mbox{if}~y_{T}\neq\texttt{EOS}\end{cases}. (11)

This ensures that πq​(EOS|𝒔T)=1\pi_{q}(\texttt{EOS}|{\bm{s}}_{T})=1, which in turn ensures that the ARM defines a valid probability distribution over all possible sequences of size at most TT. See Appendix A.1 for more details and a proof.

Analogy with EBMs.

We now rewrite the equations in order to build an analogy with EBMs. We define the “log-partition” along the sequence (path) 𝒚{\bm{y}} given 𝒙{\bm{x}} as

Aqarm​(𝒙,𝒚)≔∑t=1|𝒚|Vq​(𝒙⊕𝒚<t)=∑t=1|𝒚|LSEyt′∈𝒜​q​(𝒙⊕𝒚<t,yt′).A^{\textsc{arm}}_{q}({\bm{x}},{\bm{y}})\coloneqq\sum_{t=1}^{|{\bm{y}}|}V_{q}({\bm{x}}\oplus{\bm{y}}_{<t})=\sum_{t=1}^{|{\bm{y}}|}\underset{y^{\prime}_{t}\in{\mathcal{A}}}{{\mathrm{LSE}}}~q({\bm{x}}\oplus{\bm{y}}_{<t},y^{\prime}_{t}). (12)

Mirroring the EBM notation, we then have

pqarm​(𝒚|𝒙)=exp⁡(Rq​(𝒙,𝒚)−Aarm​(𝒙,𝒚)),p^{\textsc{arm}}_{q}({\bm{y}}|{\bm{x}})=\exp(R_{q}({\bm{x}},{\bm{y}})-A^{\textsc{arm}}({\bm{x}},{\bm{y}})), (13)

where

Rq​(𝒙,𝒚)≔∑t=1|𝒚|q⁡(𝒙⊕𝒚<t,yt).R_{q}({\bm{x}},{\bm{y}})\coloneqq\sum_{t=1}^{|{\bm{y}}|}q({\bm{x}}\oplus{\bm{y}}_{<t},y_{t}). (14)

Sampling.

To draw an i.i.d. sequence Y∼pqarm(⋅|𝒙)Y\sim p^{\textsc{arm}}_{q}(\cdot|{\bm{x}}), we can use autoregressive (a.k.a. ancestral) sampling,

Yt∼πq(⋅|St),Y_{t}\sim\pi_{q}(\cdot|S_{t}), (15)

where S1≔𝒙S_{1}\coloneqq{\bm{x}} and St≔𝒙⊕Y<tS_{t}\coloneqq{\bm{x}}\oplus Y_{<t} for t>1t>1. The sampling is repeated until an EOS token is emitted.

Learning qq from data using Transformers.

To learn qq from data, we must use a model that can score a next token yty_{t} using only the past context 𝒔t{\bm{s}}_{t}, which has variable length. This can be achieved using a causal Transformer 𝒯{\mathcal{T}}, which uses an attention mask to ensure that each token can only attend to previous tokens. The causal Transformer outputs a vector of logits 𝒉t=𝒯⁡(𝒔t)∈ℝ|𝒜|{\bm{h}}_{t}={\mathcal{T}}({\bm{s}}_{t})\in{\mathbb{R}}^{|{\mathcal{A}}|}. Intuitively, 𝒯​(𝒔t)​[yt]{\mathcal{T}}({\bm{s}}_{t})[y_{t}] can be interpreted as the score of token yt∈𝒜y_{t}\in{\mathcal{A}} given the context 𝒔t{\bm{s}}_{t}. We can therefore define q⁡(𝒔t,yt)≔𝒯⁡(𝒔t)​[yt].q({\bm{s}}_{t},y_{t})\coloneqq{\mathcal{T}}({\bm{s}}_{t})[y_{t}].

MaxEnt RL as distilling an EBM into an ARM.

We saw that the optimal solution of the regularized RL problem (5) is exactly an EBM. This creates a paradox: if we know the optimal solution, why cannot we use the EBM directly at inference time and why do we even need RL-based training? Unfortunately, as we discussed, sampling from an EBM in combinatorially-large spaces is typically intractable, often requiring Markov-chain Monte-Carlo (MCMC) methods. Therefore, (5) is often reformulated as

argmaxq∈ℱ⁡(𝒮×𝒜)𝔼X𝔼YR(X,Y)−KL(parmq(⋅|X),pref(⋅|X))\displaystyle\argmax_{q\in{\mathcal{F}}({\mathcal{S}}\times{\mathcal{A}})}{\mathbb{E}}_{X}{\mathbb{E}}_{Y}R(X,Y)-\mathrm{KL}(p^{\textsc{arm}}_{q}(\cdot|X),p_{\mathrm{ref}}(\cdot|X)) (16)
=\displaystyle= argmin𝔼XKL(parmq(⋅|X),pebmR+Rref(⋅|X))\displaystyle\argmin{\mathbb{E}}_{X}\mathrm{KL}(p^{\textsc{arm}}_{q}(\cdot|X),p^{\textsc{ebm}}_{R+R_{\mathrm{ref}}}(\cdot|X))

where YY above is distributed according to pqarm(⋅|X)p^{\textsc{arm}}_{q}(\cdot|X).

Intuitively, instead of performing maximization in the space 𝒫⁡(𝒴|𝒳){\mathcal{P}}({\mathcal{Y}}|{\mathcal{X}}) of all possible distributions, we perform maximization in the space of ARMs parameterized by a function q∈ℱ⁡(𝒮×𝒜)q\in{\mathcal{F}}({\mathcal{S}}\times{\mathcal{A}}). Thus, we can see RL-based language model post-training as approximating the EBM pR+Rrefebm(⋅|𝒙)p^{\textsc{ebm}}_{R+R_{\mathrm{ref}}}(\cdot|{\bm{x}}) with the ARM pqarm(⋅|𝒙)p^{\textsc{arm}}_{q}(\cdot|{\bm{x}}), or put differently, as distilling this EBM into this ARM.

3 From the chain rule to Bellman equations

3.1 Bijection between distributions

The chain rule of probability factorizes a joint probability distribution into a product of conditional probabilities. In this section, we show how it can be used to derive a procedure for converting any sequence distribution p∈𝒫⁡(𝒴|𝒳)p\in{\mathcal{P}}({\mathcal{Y}}|{\mathcal{X}}) to a next-token distribution π∈𝒫⁡(𝒜|𝒮)\pi\in{\mathcal{P}}({\mathcal{A}}|{\mathcal{S}}), and vice-versa.

From sequence to next-token distributions.

For any 𝒙∈𝒳{\bm{x}}\in{\mathcal{X}} and any 𝒚∈𝒴{\bm{y}}\in{\mathcal{Y}} such that |𝒚|=τ|{\bm{y}}|=\tau, with 1≤τ≤T1\leq\tau\leq T, the procedure works by successively marginalizing and conditioning in backward order. First, starting from p⁡(𝒚≤τ|𝒙)≔p⁡(𝒚|𝒙)p({\bm{y}}_{\leq\tau}|{\bm{x}})\coloneqq p({\bm{y}}|{\bm{x}}), we define from t=τ−1t=\tau-1 to t=1t=1,

p⁡(𝒚≤t|𝒙)≔∑yt+1∈𝒜p⁡(𝒚≤t,yt+1|𝒙).p({\bm{y}}_{\leq t}|{\bm{x}})\coloneqq\sum_{y_{t+1}\in{\mathcal{A}}}p({\bm{y}}_{\leq t},y_{t+1}|{\bm{x}}). (17)

Second, we define from t=τt=\tau to t=2t=2

π⁡(yt|𝒙,𝒚<t)≔p⁡(𝒚≤t|𝒙)p⁡(𝒚≤t−1|𝒙),\pi(y_{t}|{\bm{x}},{\bm{y}}_{<t})\coloneqq\frac{p({\bm{y}}_{\leq t}|{\bm{x}})}{p({\bm{y}}_{\leq t-1}|{\bm{x}})}, (18)

ending with π⁡(y1|𝒙)≔p⁡(y1|𝒙)\pi(y_{1}|{\bm{x}})\coloneqq p(y_{1}|{\bm{x}}).

From next-token to sequence distributions.

Conversely, from any next-token distribution π∈𝒫⁡(𝒜|𝒮)\pi\in{\mathcal{P}}({\mathcal{A}}|{\mathcal{S}}), we can reconstruct a sequence distribution p∈𝒫⁡(𝒴|𝒳)p\in{\mathcal{P}}({\mathcal{Y}}|{\mathcal{X}}) by

p⁡(𝒚|𝒙)=∏t=1|𝒚|π⁡(yt|𝒙,𝒚<t).p({\bm{y}}|{\bm{x}})=\prod_{t=1}^{|{\bm{y}}|}\pi(y_{t}|{\bm{x}},{\bm{y}}_{<t}). (19)

Indeed, by substituting the definition of π\pi, we observe that the product forms a telescoping sequence that exactly recovers the joint distribution: ∏t=1|𝒚|π⁡(yt|𝒙,𝒚<t)=p⁡(𝒚≤1|𝒙)1×p⁡(𝒚≤2|𝒙)p⁡(𝒚≤1|𝒙)×⋯×p⁡(𝒚≤τ|𝒙)p⁡(𝒚≤τ−1|𝒙)=p⁡(𝒚|𝒙)\prod_{t=1}^{|{\bm{y}}|}\pi(y_{t}|{\bm{x}},{\bm{y}}_{<t})=\frac{p({\bm{y}}_{\leq 1}|{\bm{x}})}{1}\times\frac{p({\bm{y}}_{\leq 2}|{\bm{x}})}{p({\bm{y}}_{\leq 1}|{\bm{x}})}\times\dots\times\frac{p({\bm{y}}_{\leq\tau}|{\bm{x}})}{p({\bm{y}}_{\leq\tau-1}|{\bm{x}})}=p({\bm{y}}|{\bm{x}}).

The chain rule of probability as a bijection.

Since there is a unique correspondence between pp and π\pi, the procedure defines a bijection between 𝒫⁡(𝒴|𝒳){\mathcal{P}}({\mathcal{Y}}|{\mathcal{X}}) and 𝒫⁡(𝒜|𝒮){\mathcal{P}}({\mathcal{A}}|{\mathcal{S}}).

3.2 Bijection in function space

We now instantiate the bijection for EBMs and ARMs, which can be seen as using sequence and next-token Gibbs (Boltzmann) distributions, respectively. In this section, we assume without loss of generality that RR decomposes as

Rr​(𝒙,𝒚)≔∑t=1|𝒚|r⁡(𝒙⊕𝒚<t⏟𝒔t,yt),R_{r}({\bm{x}},{\bm{y}})\coloneqq\sum_{t=1}^{|{\bm{y}}|}r(\underbrace{{\bm{x}}\oplus{\bm{y}}_{<t}}_{{\bm{s}}_{t}},y_{t}), (20)

where r:𝒮×𝒜→ℝr\colon{\mathcal{S}}\times{\mathcal{A}}\to{\mathbb{R}} is the immediate (next-token) reward. Indeed, if RR does not naturally decompose as above, we can always assign all the non-zero reward in the last step.

We now show how to transform r:𝒮×𝒜→ℝr\colon{\mathcal{S}}\times{\mathcal{A}}\to{\mathbb{R}} used by an EBM into q:𝒮×𝒜→ℝq\colon{\mathcal{S}}\times{\mathcal{A}}\to{\mathbb{R}} used by an ARM, and vice-versa.

From EBM to ARM.

Suppose r:𝒮×𝒜→ℝr\colon{\mathcal{S}}\times{\mathcal{A}}\to{\mathbb{R}} is given. We define the mapping q=ℳ⁡(r)q={\mathcal{M}}(r) as

q⁡(𝒔t,yt)≔{r⁡(𝒔t,yt)if​yt=EOSr⁡(𝒔t,yt)+Vq​(𝒔t⊕yt)if​yt≠EOS,q({\bm{s}}_{t},y_{t})\coloneqq\begin{cases}r({\bm{s}}_{t},y_{t})&\mbox{if}~y_{t}=\texttt{EOS}\\ r({\bm{s}}_{t},y_{t})+V_{q}({\bm{s}}_{t}\oplus y_{t})&\mbox{if}~y_{t}\neq\texttt{EOS}\end{cases}, (21)

where 𝒔t∈𝒮{\bm{s}}_{t}\in{\mathcal{S}} and yt∈𝒜y_{t}\in{\mathcal{A}}. Recall that

Vq​(𝒔t⊕yt)=LSEyt+1∈𝒜​q​(𝒔t⊕yt,yt+1).V_{q}({\bm{s}}_{t}\oplus y_{t})=\underset{y_{t+1}\in{\mathcal{A}}}{{\mathrm{LSE}}}~q({\bm{s}}_{t}\oplus y_{t},y_{t+1}). (22)

We can see that q⁡(𝒔t,⋅)q({\bm{s}}_{t},\cdot) depends on q⁡(𝒔t+1,⋅)q({\bm{s}}_{t+1},\cdot), creating a recursive dependency. Computing qq from rr must thus be done sequentially from t=τt=\tau to t=1t=1 for all possible states.

From ARM to EBM.

Suppose q:𝒮×𝒜→ℝq\colon{\mathcal{S}}\times{\mathcal{A}}\to{\mathbb{R}} is now given. We define the inverse mapping r=ℳ−1​(q)r={\mathcal{M}}^{-1}(q) as

r⁡(𝒔t,yt)≔{q⁡(𝒔t,yt)if​yt=EOSq⁡(𝒔t,yt)−Vq​(𝒔t⊕yt)if​yt≠EOS.r({\bm{s}}_{t},y_{t})\coloneqq\begin{cases}q({\bm{s}}_{t},y_{t})&\mbox{if}~y_{t}=\texttt{EOS}\\ q({\bm{s}}_{t},y_{t})-V_{q}({\bm{s}}_{t}\oplus y_{t})&\mbox{if}~y_{t}\neq\texttt{EOS}\end{cases}. (23)

As there is no longer a recursive dependency, computing rr from qq can be done in parallel.

Bijection.

Having defined the mapping ℳ{\mathcal{M}} and its inverse ℳ−1{\mathcal{M}}^{-1}, we can now formally state our result.

{proposition}

[Bijection in function space] The mapping q=ℳ⁡(r)q={\mathcal{M}}(r) is bijective and for all 𝒙∈𝒳{\bm{x}}\in{\mathcal{X}} and 𝒚∈𝒴{\bm{y}}\in{\mathcal{Y}}, we have

pRrebm​(𝒚|𝒙)\displaystyle p^{\textsc{ebm}}_{R_{r}}({\bm{y}}|{\bm{x}}) =pqarm​(𝒚|𝒙)\displaystyle=p^{\textsc{arm}}_{q}({\bm{y}}|{\bm{x}}) (24)
ARrebm​(𝒙)\displaystyle A^{\textsc{ebm}}_{R_{r}}({\bm{x}}) =Vq​(𝒙).\displaystyle=V_{q}({\bm{x}}). (25)

A proof is given in Appendix B.2. This shows that an EBM can be transformed into an ARM if rr is “corrected” by adding the log-partition VqV_{q} of the next states. In MaxEnt RL terminology (see Section 3.3 for more details), VqV_{q} is known as the soft value function and Vq​(𝒔t)V_{q}({\bm{s}}_{t}) captures the future (soft) value of being in state 𝒔t{\bm{s}}_{t}. Accordingly, since an ARM has the capacity to learn an EBM, which is a globally normalized distribution, an ARM inherently has the ability to look ahead, provided that we can learn qq appropriately.

Computational cost.

The cost of converting an ARM to an EBM is O⁡(V​T)O(VT), linear in the sequence length. On the other hand, the cost of converting an EBM into an ARM is O⁡(VT)O(V^{T}), exponential in the sequence length. Explicitly converting an EBM into an ARM is therefore intractable. However, as we shall discuss in Section 4.1, when learning from (𝒙,𝒚)({\bm{x}},{\bm{y}}) pairs, such an explicit conversion is not needed, as the optimal ARM is implicitly an EBM!

3.3 Maximum-entropy RL perspective

Autoregressive models as MDPs.

Let 𝒮{\mathcal{S}} be the set of states and 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} be the set of actions. ARMs can be seen as a special case of Markov decision processes (MDPs) where

  • •

    states are contexts: 𝒔t≔𝒙⊕𝒚<t∈𝒮{\bm{s}}_{t}\coloneqq{\bm{x}}\oplus{\bm{y}}_{<t}\in{\mathcal{S}};

  • •

    actions are tokens: yt∈𝒜y_{t}\in{\mathcal{A}};

  • •

    next states append the last token: 𝒔t+1≔𝒔t⊕yt{\bm{s}}_{t+1}\coloneqq{\bm{s}}_{t}\oplus y_{t};

  • •

    horizon is finite and there is no decay factor (γ=1\gamma=1);

  • •

    rr is the immediate reward function.

From this perspective, an ARM is a particular instance of a MDP, where the transition kernel μ(⋅|𝒔t,yt)\mu(\cdot|{\bm{s}}_{t},y_{t}) is deterministic with μ⁡(𝒔t⊕yt|𝒔t,yt)=1\mu({\bm{s}}_{t}\oplus y_{t}|{\bm{s}}_{t},y_{t})=1. These particularly simple state transition dynamics imply that each state is never visited more than once. This perspective should not be confused with the (combinatorial) contextual bandit perspective, where 𝒙{\bm{x}} corresponds to the single state, 𝒚{\bm{y}} corresponds to an action and RR is the sequence-level reward function.

Soft Bellman equation. In MaxEnt RL, we seek the policy

π⋆=argmaxπ∈𝒫⁡(𝒜|𝒮)𝔼​∑t=1∞γt​(r⁡(St,At)−log⁡π⁡(At|St)).\pi^{\star}=\argmax_{\pi\in{\mathcal{P}}({\mathcal{A}}|{\mathcal{S}})}{\mathbb{E}}\sum_{t=1}^{\infty}\gamma^{t}(r(S_{t},A_{t})-\log\pi(A_{t}|S_{t})). (26)

The expectation is over trajectories of state-action pairs starting from S1∼p𝒳S_{1}\sim p_{\mathcal{X}} and following

At\displaystyle A_{t} ∼π(⋅|St)\displaystyle\sim\pi(\cdot|S_{t}) (27)
St+1\displaystyle S_{t+1} ∼μ(⋅|St,At).\displaystyle\sim\mu(\cdot|S_{t},A_{t}). (28)

It is well-known in this literature (see Section 6 for a detailed review) that an optimal solution is

π⋆​(a|𝒔)=exp⁡(q⋆​(𝒔,a)−Vq⋆​(𝒔))\pi^{\star}(a|{\bm{s}})=\exp(q^{\star}({\bm{s}},a)-V_{q^{\star}}({\bm{s}})) (29)

where q⋆q^{\star} is a solution of the fixed point equation

q(𝒔,a)=r(𝒔,a)+γ𝔼S∼μ(⋅|𝒔,a)Vq(S).q({\bm{s}},a)=r({\bm{s}},a)+\gamma{\mathbb{E}}_{S\sim\mu(\cdot|{\bm{s}},a)}V_{q}(S). (30)

Existence and uniqueness of the fixed point.

In the general RL setting (infinite horizon, cyclic MDPs), the existence and uniqueness of the fixed point q⋆q^{\star} rely on the Banach fixed point theorem. The standard condition is simply γ<1\gamma<1, which guarantees that the soft Bellman operator (ℬrq)(𝒔,a)≔r(𝒔,a)+γ𝔼S∼μ(⋅|𝒔,a)Vq(S)(\mathcal{B}_{r}q)({\bm{s}},a)\coloneqq r({\bm{s}},a)+\gamma{\mathbb{E}}_{S\sim\mu(\cdot|{\bm{s}},a)}V_{q}(S) is a contractive mapping. Typically, q⋆q^{\star} does not enjoy an explicit formula and finding q⋆q^{\star} requires some form of fixed point iterations. In contrast, in our setting (finite horizon, acyclic MDP), q⋆=ℳ⁡(r)q^{\star}={\mathcal{M}}(r) is the explicit formula of the fixed point solution, which guarantees both existence and uniqueness (invertibility). Moreover, we constructed the bijection through the chain rule of probability, unraveling a deep connection with the soft Bellman equation in our particular setting.

3.4 Entropy-regularized DP on a DAG perspective

We can also view our bijection as regularized dynamic programming (DP) on a directed acyclic graph (DAG). In this perspective, we define a DAG where

  • •

    there is one start (root) node corresponding to 𝒔1=𝒙{\bm{s}}_{1}={\bm{x}};

  • •

    there is one end node;

  • •

    intermediate nodes are contexts 𝒔t≔𝒙⊕𝒚<t{\bm{s}}_{t}\coloneqq{\bm{x}}\oplus{\bm{y}}_{<t};

  • •

    edge weights indicate the value r⁡(𝒔t,yt)r({\bm{s}}_{t},y_{t}) of appending yty_{t} to context 𝒔t{\bm{s}}_{t} (higher is better);

  • •

    nodes such that 𝒔t≔𝒙⊕(y1,…,EOS){\bm{s}}_{t}\coloneqq{\bm{x}}\oplus(y_{1},\dots,\texttt{EOS}) have a single out-going edge of weight 00, connected to the end node.

Computing max⁡∑t=1|𝒚|𝒚∈𝒴⁡r⁡(𝒙⊕𝒚<t,yt)\max_{{\bm{y}}\in{\mathcal{Y}}}\sum_{t=1}^{|{\bm{y}}|}r({\bm{x}}\oplus{\bm{y}}_{<t},y_{t}) then amounts to finding the path in the DAG of maximum value and computing the log-partition ARrebm​(𝒙)=LSE𝒚∈𝒴​∑t=1|𝒚|r⁡(𝒙⊕𝒚<t,yt)A^{\textsc{ebm}}_{R_{r}}({\bm{x}})=\underset{{\bm{y}}\in{\mathcal{Y}}}{{\mathrm{LSE}}}~\sum_{t=1}^{|{\bm{y}}|}r({\bm{x}}\oplus{\bm{y}}_{<t},y_{t}) amounts to finding the path of soft maximum value.

Top-down vs. bottom-up DP.

To compute the soft-maximum ARrebm​(𝒙)=Vq​(𝒙)A^{\textsc{ebm}}_{R_{r}}({\bm{x}})=V_{q}({\bm{x}}) for q=ℳ⁡(r)q={\mathcal{M}}(r) by DP, two approaches are possible. In top-down DP, we start from Vq​(𝒙)V_{q}({\bm{x}}), the quantity we wish to compute, and recurse. This corresponds to traversing the DAG forward in time. In bottom-up DP (tabulation), we start from the base cases and make our way up to Vq​(𝒙)V_{q}({\bm{x}}). This corresponds to traversing the DAG backward in time. As shown in (Mensch & Blondel, 2018), the associativity of the log-sum-exp and of the distributivity of ++ over the log-sum-exp guarantee the optimality of dynamic programming. Indeed, we have (fixing |𝒚|=T|{\bm{y}}|=T to simplify the notation)

ARrebm​(𝒙)\displaystyle A^{\textsc{ebm}}_{R_{r}}({\bm{x}}) =LSE𝒚∈𝒴​∑t=1Tr⁡(𝒙⊕𝒚<t,yt)\displaystyle=\underset{{\bm{y}}\in{\mathcal{Y}}}{{\mathrm{LSE}}}~\sum_{t=1}^{T}r({\bm{x}}\oplus{\bm{y}}_{<t},y_{t}) (31)
=LSEy1∈𝒱​…​LSEyT∈𝒱​∑t=1Tr⁡(𝒙⊕𝒚<t,yt)\displaystyle=\underset{y_{1}\in{\mathcal{V}}}{{\mathrm{LSE}}}\dots\underset{y_{T}\in{\mathcal{V}}}{{\mathrm{LSE}}}~\sum_{t=1}^{T}r({\bm{x}}\oplus{\bm{y}}_{<t},y_{t}) (32)
=LSEy1∈𝒱​[r⁡(𝒙,y1)+⋯+LSEyT∈𝒱​[r⁡(𝒙⊕𝒚<T,yT)]].\displaystyle=\underset{y_{1}\in{\mathcal{V}}}{{\mathrm{LSE}}}~\biggl[r({\bm{x}},y_{1})+\dots+\underset{y_{T}\in{\mathcal{V}}}{{\mathrm{LSE}}}~\Bigl[r({\bm{x}}\oplus{\bm{y}}_{<T},y_{T})\Bigr]\biggr]. (33)

It is well-known that the gradient of the log-partition exactly coincides with marginal probabilities (Wainwright et al., 2008). In Appendix A.11, we show that the gradient w.r.t. rr of ARrebm​(𝒙)=Vq​(𝒙)A^{\textsc{ebm}}_{R_{r}}({\bm{x}})=V_{q}({\bm{x}}) for q=ℳ⁡(r)q={\mathcal{M}}(r) indeed exactly coincides with the marginal probabilities of response prefixes.

4 Theoretical analysis

4.1 Learning EBMs and ARMs from input-output pairs

In this section, building upon our bijection in Section 3.2, we state equivalence results between learning EBMs and learning ARMs from (𝒙,𝒚)({\bm{x}},{\bm{y}}) pairs.

Negative log-likelihood of EBMs.

The negative log-likelihood of 𝒚{\bm{y}} given 𝒙{\bm{x}} according to pRebmp^{\textsc{ebm}}_{R} is

ℓRebm​(𝒙,𝒚)≔−log⁡pRebm​(𝒚|𝒙)=ARebm​(𝒙)−R⁡(𝒙,𝒚).\ell^{\textsc{ebm}}_{R}({\bm{x}},{\bm{y}})\coloneqq-\log p^{\textsc{ebm}}_{R}({\bm{y}}|{\bm{x}})=A^{\textsc{ebm}}_{R}({\bm{x}})-R({\bm{x}},{\bm{y}}). (34)

The loss is convex in RR and satisfies the property

ℓRebm​(𝒙,𝒚)=0⇔pRebm​(𝒚|𝒙)=1.\ell^{\textsc{ebm}}_{R}({\bm{x}},{\bm{y}})=0\iff p^{\textsc{ebm}}_{R}({\bm{y}}|{\bm{x}})=1. (35)

Negative log-likelihood of ARMs.

The negative log-likelihood of 𝒚{\bm{y}} given 𝒙{\bm{x}} according to pqarmp^{\textsc{arm}}_{q} is

ℓqarm​(𝒙,𝒚)\displaystyle\ell^{\textsc{arm}}_{q}({\bm{x}},{\bm{y}}) ≔−log⁡pqarm​(𝒚|𝒙)\displaystyle\coloneqq-\log p^{\textsc{arm}}_{q}({\bm{y}}|{\bm{x}}) (36)
=Aarm​(𝒙,𝒚)−Rq​(𝒙,𝒚).\displaystyle=A^{\textsc{arm}}({\bm{x}},{\bm{y}})-R_{q}({\bm{x}},{\bm{y}}). (37)

The loss is convex in qq and satisfies the property

ℓqarm​(𝒙,𝒚)=0⇔pqarm​(𝒚|𝒙)=1.\ell^{\textsc{arm}}_{q}({\bm{x}},{\bm{y}})=0\iff p^{\textsc{arm}}_{q}({\bm{y}}|{\bm{x}})=1. (38)

Unlike AebmA^{\textsc{ebm}}, AarmA^{\textsc{arm}} is a function of 𝒙{\bm{x}} and 𝒚{\bm{y}}, not just 𝒙{\bm{x}}. Therefore, contrary to EBMs, the negative log-likelihood of an ARM is using the ground-truth sequence 𝒚{\bm{y}} as a path. This is known as teacher forcing. Despite what the name may suggest, this behavior arises naturally as a consequence of using negative log-likelihood on ARMs.

Equivalence of minima.

Let us define the expected risks

ℒarm​(q)\displaystyle{\mathcal{L}}^{\textsc{arm}}(q) ≔𝔼(X,Y)∼ρ​[ℓqarm​(X,Y)]\displaystyle\coloneqq{\mathbb{E}}_{(X,Y)\sim\rho}\left[\ell^{\textsc{arm}}_{q}(X,Y)\right] (39)
ℒebm​(R)\displaystyle{\mathcal{L}}^{\textsc{ebm}}(R) ≔𝔼(X,Y)∼ρ​[ℓRebm​(X,Y)].\displaystyle\coloneqq{\mathbb{E}}_{(X,Y)\sim\rho}\left[\ell^{\textsc{ebm}}_{R}(X,Y)\right]. (40)

We then have the following equivalence, which is a straightforward consequence of our bijection in Section 3.2. {proposition}[Equivalence of minima]

For any joint distribution ρ\rho over 𝒳×𝒴{\mathcal{X}}\times{\mathcal{Y}}, we have

minq∈ℱ⁡(𝒮×𝒜)⁡ℒarm​(q)\displaystyle\min_{q\in{\mathcal{F}}({\mathcal{S}}\times{\mathcal{A}})}{\mathcal{L}}^{\textsc{arm}}(q) =minr∈ℱ⁡(𝒮×𝒜)⁡ℒebm​(Rr)\displaystyle=\min_{r\in{\mathcal{F}}({\mathcal{S}}\times{\mathcal{A}})}{\mathcal{L}}^{\textsc{ebm}}(R_{r}) (41)
=minR∈ℱ⁡(𝒳×𝒴)⁡ℒebm​(R)\displaystyle=\min_{R\in{\mathcal{F}}({\mathcal{X}}\times{\mathcal{Y}})}{\mathcal{L}}^{\textsc{ebm}}(R) (42)

and, with q⋆=ℳ⁡(r⋆)q^{\star}={\mathcal{M}}(r^{\star}), we have

q⋆∈argminq∈ℱ⁡(𝒮×𝒜)ℒarm​(q)\displaystyle q^{\star}\in\argmin_{q\in{\mathcal{F}}({\mathcal{S}}\times{\mathcal{A}})}{\mathcal{L}}^{\textsc{arm}}(q) ⇔r⋆∈argminr∈ℱ⁡(𝒮×𝒜)ℒebm​(Rr)\displaystyle\iff r^{\star}\in\argmin_{r\in{\mathcal{F}}({\mathcal{S}}\times{\mathcal{A}})}{\mathcal{L}}^{\textsc{ebm}}(R_{r}) (43)
⟹Rr⋆∈argminR∈ℱ⁡(𝒳×𝒴)ℒebm​(R).\displaystyle\implies R_{r^{\star}}\in\argmin_{R\in{\mathcal{F}}({\mathcal{X}}\times{\mathcal{Y}})}{\mathcal{L}}^{\textsc{ebm}}(R). (44)

See Appendix B.3 for a proof. Proposition 4.1 shows that, when the goal is to fit a model to observed input-output pairs (𝒙,𝒚)({\bm{x}},{\bm{y}}) by negative log-likelihood minimization, EBMs and ARMs are equivalently powerful, provided that we perform minimization in function space, which means that the functions are able to fit the data perfectly.

Optimality of teacher forcing.

Learning the reward RR from data corresponds to an inverse RL setting (Ziebart et al., 2008). From a duality perspective (Sander et al., 2025), the optimal primal variable R⋆R^{\star} is linked to the optimal dual variable p⋆p^{\star} through, for all 𝒙∈𝒳{\bm{x}}\in{\mathcal{X}},

p⋆(⋅|𝒙)=softargmax(R⋆(𝒙,⋅))=pR⋆ebm(⋅|𝒙).p^{\star}(\cdot|{\bm{x}})=\mathrm{softargmax}(R^{\star}({\bm{x}},\cdot))=p^{\textsc{ebm}}_{R^{\star}}(\cdot|{\bm{x}}). (45)

Unfortunately, recovering p⋆p^{\star} from R⋆R^{\star} is difficult, due to the intractable normalization constant. However, given q⋆q^{\star} (the optimal solution via teacher forcing), p⋆p^{\star} can be constructed from πq⋆\pi_{q^{\star}} using the chain rule of probability in (19),

p⋆​(𝒚|𝒙)=∏t=1|𝒚|πq⋆​(yt|𝒙,𝒚<t).p^{\star}({\bm{y}}|{\bm{x}})=\prod_{t=1}^{|{\bm{y}}|}\pi_{q^{\star}}(y_{t}|{\bm{x}},{\bm{y}}_{<t}). (46)

This demonstrates that teacher forcing is optimal when optimizing in function space. We stress that the mapping ℳ{\mathcal{M}} is completely implicit in this case (we do not need to explicitly compute it). We summarize the mappings in Figure 1.

4.2 Distilling EBMs into ARMs

We saw in Section 2 that KL-regularized RL can be seen as distilling EBMs into ARMs. This motivates the need for approximation guarantees of EBMs by ARMs.

Function space.

Stated differently, Proposition 3.2 shows that the exact mapping q=ℳ⁡(r)q={\mathcal{M}}(r) satisfies for all 𝒙∈𝒳{\bm{x}}\in{\mathcal{X}}

KL(pqarm(⋅|𝒙),pRrebm(⋅|𝒙))=0.{\mathrm{KL}}(p^{\textsc{arm}}_{q}(\cdot|{\bm{x}}),p^{\textsc{ebm}}_{R_{r}}(\cdot|{\bm{x}}))=0. (47)

Such a result holds in function space. This is the so-called tabular setting in RL, where the functions q:𝒮×𝒜→ℝq\colon{\mathcal{S}}\times{\mathcal{A}}\to{\mathbb{R}} and r:𝒮×𝒜→ℝr\colon{\mathcal{S}}\times{\mathcal{A}}\to{\mathbb{R}} are represented as (gigantic) arrays, exploiting the fact that the space of contexts (states) 𝒮{\mathcal{S}} and the space of next tokens 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} are finite.

Function approximation setting.

In practice, qq and rr are implemented using parameterized functions. In this setting, there may no longer be an exact conversion between EBMs and ARMs, but we can bound their KL divergence. {proposition}[KL bound] For all r:𝒮×𝒜→ℝr\colon{\mathcal{S}}\times{\mathcal{A}}\to{\mathbb{R}}, q:𝒮×𝒜→ℝq\colon{\mathcal{S}}\times{\mathcal{A}}\to{\mathbb{R}} and 𝒙∈𝒳{\bm{x}}\in{\mathcal{X}}, we have

KL(pqarm(⋅|𝒙),pRrebm(⋅|𝒙))≤2Tmax𝒔∈𝒮⁡(𝒙)y∈𝒜|q⋆(𝒔,y)−q(𝒔,y)|,{\mathrm{KL}}(p^{\textsc{arm}}_{q}(\cdot|{\bm{x}}),p^{\textsc{ebm}}_{R_{r}}(\cdot|{\bm{x}}))\leq 2T\max_{\begin{subarray}{c}{\bm{s}}\in{\mathcal{S}}({\bm{x}})\\ y\in{\mathcal{A}}\end{subarray}}|q^{\star}({\bm{s}},y)-q({\bm{s}},y)|, (48)

where q⋆≔ℳ⁡(r)q^{\star}\coloneqq{\mathcal{M}}(r). A proof is given in Appendix B.4. Note that the KL divergence is not symmetric but the same bound also applies for KL(pRrebm(⋅|𝒙),pqarm(⋅|𝒙)){\mathrm{KL}}(p^{\textsc{ebm}}_{R_{r}}(\cdot|{\bm{x}}),p^{\textsc{arm}}_{q}(\cdot|{\bm{x}})).

Approximation using a Transformer.

For a fixed EBM parameterized by RrR_{r}, let q⋆=ℳ⁡(r)q^{\star}={\mathcal{M}}(r). We now show that q⋆q^{\star} can be approximated by a causal Transformer model by leveraging a powerful approximation result of causal mappings by causal Transformers (Furuya et al., 2025, Theorem 2). More precisely, for all ε>0\varepsilon>0, there exists a causal Transformer 𝒯:𝒮→ℝ|𝒜|\mathcal{T}:{\mathcal{S}}\to{\mathbb{R}}^{|{\mathcal{A}}|} such that, for all 𝒙∈𝒳{\bm{x}}\in{\mathcal{X}},

max𝒔∈𝒮⁡(𝒙),y∈𝒜⁡|q⋆​(𝒔,y)−𝒯⁡(𝒔)​[y]|≤ε.\max_{\begin{subarray}{c}{\bm{s}}\in{\mathcal{S}}({\bm{x}}),y\in{\mathcal{A}}\end{subarray}}|q^{\star}({\bm{s}},y)-\mathcal{T}({\bm{s}})[y]|\leq\varepsilon. (49)

Together with Proposition 4.2, this gives for all 𝒙∈𝒳{\bm{x}}\in{\mathcal{X}},

KL(p𝒯(.)[.]arm(⋅|𝒙),pRrebm(⋅|𝒙))≤2Tε.{\mathrm{KL}}(p^{\textsc{arm}}_{\mathcal{T}(.)[.]}(\cdot|{\bm{x}}),p^{\textsc{ebm}}_{R_{r}}(\cdot|{\bm{x}}))\leq 2T\varepsilon. (50)

However, this result requires the embedding dimension of 𝒯{\mathcal{T}} to scale with the vocabulary size |𝒱||\mathcal{V}| (Furuya et al., 2025).

5 Numerical validation

In this section, we validate our theory using synthetic tiny language models. We focus on small vocabulary VV and small maximum length TT , enabling exact computation of the EBM’s log-partition, without resorting to approximate algorithms. We minimize the expected risks in (39) and (40), using a non-causal Transformer for the EBM and a causal Transformer for the ARM. The minimum risk is defined as ℒ⋆≔−𝔼(X,Y)∼ρ​log⁡ρ⁡(X,Y){\mathcal{L}}^{\star}\coloneqq-{\mathbb{E}}_{(X,Y)\sim\rho}\log\rho(X,Y). All experimental details are included in Appendix C.

In Figure 2 (left), we plot the optimality gap ℒ−ℒ⋆{\mathcal{L}}-{\mathcal{L}}^{\star} of both the EBM and the ARM as a function of optimization steps. Our results confirm that the EBM and ARM converge to the same minima, as predicted by Proposition 4.1. Perhaps more surprisingly, our results also show that the loss curves of both models are very close, during the entire training course. These findings are confirmed across several model sizes, and sequence-length / vocabulary ratios (Appendix C).

In Figure 2 (right), we show the L∞L_{\infty} distance between the logits of the trained ARM and the logits of the optimal EBM, before and after applying the mapping ℳ{\mathcal{M}}. Our results therefore confirm that the mapping ℳ{\mathcal{M}} can be used to explicitly convert the logits of the EBM and ARM. However, we emphasize that explicit logit conversion is not needed, since we can also factorize the EBM distribution using (46).

6 Related work

Maximum-entropy RL.

Maximum entropy was used for inverse RL, where the goal is to recover the reward function from offline trajectories (Ziebart et al., 2008). In the forward setting, a precursor is dynamic policy programming (Azar et al., 2012). Many papers subsequently formally established the equivalence between policy-based methods, that seek to solve (26) w.r.t. π\pi, and value-based methods, that seek to satisfy (30) w.r.t. qq (O’Donoghue et al., 2017; Haarnoja et al., 2017; Nachum et al., 2017; Schulman et al., 2017). The equivalence was revisited in continuous action space using convex duality (Richemond & Maginnis, 2017). Entropy-regularized RL was further studied (Neu et al., 2017) and extended to other strongly-convex regularizers (Geist et al., 2019). Several papers proposed one-step and multi-step consistency loss functions based on applying the squared loss to the optimality condition (30) (Nachum et al., 2017; Schulman et al., 2017; Clavier et al., 2025). Several papers proposed soft actor-critic algorithms (O’Donoghue et al., 2017; Haarnoja et al., 2017; Haarnoja et al., 2018) or joint learning of the policy and value function (Richemond et al., 2024).

RL as probabilistic inference.

Maxent RL can be viewed from a probabilistic inference perspective, using undirected graphical models (Toussaint et al., 2009; Ziebart, 2010), defining EBMs (a.k.a. conditional random fields), or directed graphical models, mirroring hidden Markov models (Attias, 2003; Levine, 2018). Notably, this connection has been leveraged to solve inference problems using MCTS and learned soft value functions (Buesing et al., 2020). Conversely, probabilistic inference tools can be leveraged for maxent RL (Korbak et al., 2022), such as twisted sequential Monte Carlo (Zhao et al., 2024). We revisit the probabilistic inference perspective in our setting in Appendix A.9.

Energy-based models.

The standard approach for learning an EBM from (𝒙,𝒚)({\bm{x}},{\bm{y}}) pairs by stochastic gradient descent requires sampling from the EBM (Song & Kingma, 2021), which usually involves MCMC algorithms such as Langevin when 𝒴{\mathcal{Y}} is continuous or Gibbs sampling when 𝒴{\mathcal{Y}} is discrete. Since that approach learns the function RR (the reward in inverse RL; see Section 4.1), and not a generative model π\pi, MCMC is needed for generating samples from the EBM parameterized by the learned RR. A min-min formulation was proposed to jointly learn RR and the log-partition AA (Sander et al., 2025). While this bypasses the need for MCMC at train time, it still requires it for sampling from the EBM. We emphasize however that if we do not need to sample but just to predict the mode of the EBM (the most likely output 𝒚{\bm{y}} given 𝒙{\bm{x}}), then we only need to maximize RR, which does not involve the log-partition and is tractable for some sets 𝒴{\mathcal{Y}}. On the other hand, min-max formulations can be used to jointly learn a discriminator (reward) RR and a generator (policy) π\pi from (𝒙,𝒚)({\bm{x}},{\bm{y}}) pairs (Ho & Ermon, 2016). Such approach does not require MCMC if the generator easily generates samples by design, as is the case with ARMs.

GFlowNets.

GFlowNets (Bengio et al., 2021; Bengio et al., 2023) can be used to perform amortized probabilistic inference (Hu et al., 2023). Flow consistency equations play the same role as soft Bellman equations, enabling the design of consistency loss functions (Malkin et al., 2022). In fact, recent work has established that GFlowNets can be cast as MaxEnt RL, even in the general DAG setting (Tiapkin et al., 2024).

Limitations of teacher forcing.

Recent work argued that the next-token prediction objective (teacher forcing) is structurally “myopic” and fails to backpropagate future value information effectively, leading to a failure in planning (Bachmann & Nagarajan, 2024). In contrast, Proposition 4.1 shows that the global minimum of the teacher forcing objective (in function space) is an EBM, which inherently performs lookahead via the partition function VqV_{q}. Our work therefore suggests that the limitation of teacher forcing is not in the objective itself but in the difficulty of reaching its minimum, due to optimization or approximation error. This aligns with prior work showing that planning failures stem from overfitting to spurious correlations under weak supervision, rather than inherent structural incapacity (Frydenlund, 2024). In complementary work, behavior cloning, the counterpart of teacher forcing in RL, was shown to achieve horizon-independent sample complexity (Foster et al., 2024).

7 Conclusion

Significance of this work.

EBMs and ARMs are usually thought as two very distinct classes of models. EBMs are globally consistent but are difficult to train and sample from, while ARMs are easy to train and sample from but are only backward looking. Our paper shows that EBMs and ARMs are in fact intimately related. Our first contribution is to establish a bijective mapping ℳ{\mathcal{M}} between EBMs and ARMs in function space. While this mapping is a special case of soft Bellman equation in general MDPs (Section 3.3) and of entropy-regularized dynamic programming in a DAG (Section 3.4), we arrive at it from a very different angle, that of the chain rule of probability (Section 3.1 and Section 3.2). When learning from (𝒙,𝒚)({\bm{x}},{\bm{y}}) pairs, Proposition 4.1 shows that, in function space, EBMs and ARMs are equivalently powerful, establishing the optimality of teacher forcing in this case. When distilling an EBM teacher into an ARM student, Proposition 4.2 shows that the KL between the EBM and the ARM is bounded by the L∞L_{\infty} norm of the bijective mapping ℳ{\mathcal{M}}. Our results, validated through numerical experiments, provide some justification for the next-token prediction paradigm and for teacher forcing.

Limitations.

When learning from (𝒙,𝒚)({\bm{x}},{\bm{y}}) pairs, Proposition 4.1 establishes that ARMs and EBMs are equally powerful when optimizing for RR and qq in function space. However, in practice, RR can be a non-causal Transformer while qq must be causal. In addition, Proposition 3.2 establishes that, in order for ARMs and EBMs to be equivalent, qq must take the form q⁡(𝒔,y)=r⁡(𝒔,y)+Vq​(𝒔⊕y)q({\bm{s}},y)=r({\bm{s}},y)+V_{q}({\bm{s}}\oplus y), where VqV_{q} represents the (soft) optimal value of all future continuations. The function qq is therefore burdened with a dual task: it must model the immediate local score rr, and it must learn to implicitly compute a potentially complex future-looking value function VqV_{q} (marginalizing over all possible futures) using only a backward-looking architecture. Proposition 4.1 does not account for optimization or approximation error. Formally comparing the complexity of learning RR versus that of learning qq is a promising future direction. Another important direction is to study the impact of latent variables (thinking traces) in enhancing the expressivity of ARMs.

Bridging communities.

This paper builds bridges between ARMs, EBMs and Maxent RL. We hope that our paper contributes to shedding additional light on how many works and perspectives relate to each other.

Impact statement

This paper studies the connection between energy-based models and autoregressive models to justify the lookahead capabilities of next-token prediction. We do not foresee any specific ethical or societal implications arising directly from this work.
