A.1 Handling variable-length sequences in ARMs

For completeness, we review here the crucial role of EOS to induce a valid probability distribution over variable-length sequences of finite size. For more details, we refer the reader to Cotterell et al. (2023, Section 2.5). See also Eisenstein (2019, Chapter 6) for a simple introduction to language models.

Probability of finished vs. unfinished responses.

Let us define the set of possible sequences up to size TT in a vocabulary 𝒱{\mathcal{V}} as 𝒱≤T≔∪t=1T𝒱t{\mathcal{V}}^{\leq T}\coloneqq\cup_{t=1}^{T}{\mathcal{V}}^{t}. We use X∈𝒳X\in{\mathcal{X}} to denote the random variable of a prompt and Y∈𝒱≤TY\in{\mathcal{V}}^{\leq T} to denote the random variable of a finished response of size at most TT. We then define the probability that a sequence 𝒚=(y1,…,yτ){\bm{y}}=(y_{1},\ldots,y_{\tau}) is a finished response given 𝒙{\bm{x}} as

ℙ⁡(Y=𝒚|X=𝒙)≔ℙ⁡(Y1=y1,…,Yτ=yτ,len⁡(Y)=τ|X=𝒙).{\mathbb{P}}(Y={\bm{y}}|X={\bm{x}})\coloneqq{\mathbb{P}}(Y_{1}=y_{1},\ldots,Y_{\tau}=y_{\tau},{\mathrm{len}}(Y)=\tau|X={\bm{x}}).

It is the probability that the first τ\tau tokens in YY are y1,…,yτy_{1},\ldots,y_{\tau} and that the sentence is of length 0≤τ≤T0\leq\tau\leq T.

This probability should not be confused with the marginal probability of an unfinished response,

ℙ⁡(Y≤τ=𝒚|X=𝒙)≔ℙ⁡(Y1=y1,…,Yτ=yτ|X=𝒙).{\mathbb{P}}(Y_{\leq\tau}={\bm{y}}|X={\bm{x}})\coloneqq{\mathbb{P}}(Y_{1}=y_{1},\ldots,Y_{\tau}=y_{\tau}|X={\bm{x}}).

It is the probability that the first τ\tau tokens in YY are y1,…,yτy_{1},\ldots,y_{\tau}, while YY is of potentially larger length. Formally, the event {Y1=y1,…,Yτ=yτ,len⁡(Y)=τ′}\{Y_{1}=y_{1},\ldots,Y_{\tau}=y_{\tau},{\mathrm{len}}(Y)=\tau^{\prime}\} for τ′>τ\tau^{\prime}>\tau is not a singleton, while the event {Y1=y1,…,Yτ=yτ,len⁡(Y)=τ}\{Y_{1}=y_{1},\ldots,Y_{\tau}=y_{\tau},{\mathrm{len}}(Y)=\tau\} does reduce to the singleton {Y=𝒚}\{Y={\bm{y}}\}. Said differently, {Y≤τ=𝒚}≠{Y=𝒚}\{Y_{\leq\tau}={\bm{y}}\}\neq\{Y={\bm{y}}\}.

Explicit length handling.

A natural way to describe finished responses of variable length would be to define a random variable L∈ℕL\in{\mathbb{N}} encoding the length and to define the distribution over fixed size sequences Y1:l|L=lY_{1:l}|L=l for l∈ℕl\in{\mathbb{N}}. Unfortunately, in an autoregressive setting, this breaks the information flow: we do not foresee the final length before starting to output tokens. Instead, autoregressive models can condition the length on the past tokens, i.e., they can decompose the probability ℙ⁡(Y=𝒚|X=𝒙){\mathbb{P}}(Y={\bm{y}}|X={\bm{x}}) as

ℙ⁡(Y=𝒚|X=𝒙)\displaystyle{\mathbb{P}}(Y={\bm{y}}|X={\bm{x}}) =ℙ⁡(Y1=y1,…,Yτ=yτ|X=𝒙)​ℙ​(len⁡(Y)=τ|X=𝒙,Y1=y1,…,Yτ=yτ)\displaystyle={\mathbb{P}}(Y_{1}=y_{1},\ldots,Y_{\tau}=y_{\tau}|X={\bm{x}}){\mathbb{P}}({\mathrm{len}}(Y)=\tau|X={\bm{x}},Y_{1}=y_{1},\ldots,Y_{\tau}=y_{\tau})
=ℙ⁡(Y1=y1|S1=𝒔1)​…​ℙ​(Yτ=yτ|Sτ=𝒔τ)​ℙ​(len⁡(Y)=τ|Sτ=𝒔τ),\displaystyle={\mathbb{P}}(Y_{1}=y_{1}|S_{1}={\bm{s}}_{1})\ldots{\mathbb{P}}(Y_{\tau}=y_{\tau}|S_{\tau}={\bm{s}}_{\tau}){\mathbb{P}}({\mathrm{len}}(Y)=\tau|S_{\tau}={\bm{s}}_{\tau}),

where we used the contexts (states) 𝒔t≔𝒙⊕𝒚<t{\bm{s}}_{t}\coloneqq{\bm{x}}\oplus{\bm{y}}_{<t} and 𝒔1=𝒙{\bm{s}}_{1}={\bm{x}}, and similarly for StS_{t} and S1S_{1}.

Implicit length handling using EOS.

This decomposition suggests a simple way to encode the length in an autoregressive model: adding a new possible output token, called EOS, such that for any t≥0t\geq 0,

ℙ⁡(Yt=EOS|St=𝒔t)=ℙ⁡(len⁡(Y)=t|St=𝒔t).{\mathbb{P}}(Y_{t}=\texttt{EOS}|S_{t}={\bm{s}}_{t})={\mathbb{P}}({\mathrm{len}}(Y)=t|S_{t}={\bm{s}}_{t}). (51)

Using this approach, finished responses should now always include EOS as the last token, and the length of a sequence now includes EOS. More formally, instead of defining Y∈𝒱≤TY\in{\mathcal{V}}^{\leq T}, we now define Y∈𝒴Y\in{\mathcal{Y}}, where 𝒴=∪t=1T(𝒱t×{EOS}){\mathcal{Y}}=\cup_{t=1}^{T}({\mathcal{V}}^{t}\times\{\texttt{EOS}\}). It should be noted that EOS is just a convenient way to encode the length and does not change the cardinality of the set of possible sequences, since

|𝒱t×{EOS}|=|𝒱t|=Vt.|{\mathcal{V}}^{t}\times\{\texttt{EOS}\}|=|{\mathcal{V}}^{t}|=V^{t}. (52)

The advantage of the EOS approach is that we can support seamlessly both the probability of finished responses (by appending EOS as last token) and the marginal probability of unfinished responses (by not appending EOS as last token). Indeed, assuming yτ≠EOSy_{\tau}\neq\texttt{EOS}, we have

ℙ⁡(Y≤τ=𝒚|X=𝒙)=ℙ⁡(Y1=y1|S1=𝒔1)​…​ℙ​(Yτ=yτ|Sτ=𝒔τ).{\mathbb{P}}(Y_{\leq\tau}={\bm{y}}|X={\bm{x}})={\mathbb{P}}(Y_{1}=y_{1}|S_{1}={\bm{s}}_{1})\ldots{\mathbb{P}}(Y_{\tau}=y_{\tau}|S_{\tau}={\bm{s}}_{\tau}). (53)

The function qq used to define πq\pi_{q} takes a (context, next-token) pair and returns a scalar-valued score. Strictly speaking, the context tokens are in the vocabulary 𝒱{\mathcal{V}} while the next token is in the augmented vocabulary 𝒜≔𝒱∪{EOS}{\mathcal{A}}\coloneqq{\mathcal{V}}\cup\{\texttt{EOS}\}. Therefore, q:𝒮×𝒜→ℝq\colon{\mathcal{S}}\times{\mathcal{A}}\to{\mathbb{R}}, where 𝒮≔∪t=1T𝒳×𝒱t{\mathcal{S}}\coloneqq\cup_{t=1}^{T}{\mathcal{X}}\times{\mathcal{V}}^{t}.

Validity of the probability distribution over sequences.

We formally give below a sufficient condition which guarantees that an ARM defines a valid probability distribution over finished responses. {proposition}[Validity of the distribution defined by an ARM]

Let 𝒴≔⋃τ=1T𝒱τ−1×{EOS}{\mathcal{Y}}\coloneqq\bigcup_{\tau=1}^{T}{\mathcal{V}}^{\tau-1}\times\{\texttt{EOS}\} be the set of valid finished responses of length at most TT. If πq​(EOS|𝒔T)=1\pi_{q}(\texttt{EOS}|{\bm{s}}_{T})=1 for all 𝒔T∈𝒳×𝒱T−1{\bm{s}}_{T}\in{\mathcal{X}}\times{\mathcal{V}}^{T-1}, then for all 𝒙∈𝒳{\bm{x}}\in{\mathcal{X}}

∑𝒚∈𝒴pqarm​(𝒚|𝒙)=1.\sum_{{\bm{y}}\in{\mathcal{Y}}}p^{\textsc{arm}}_{q}({\bm{y}}|{\bm{x}})=1. (54)

That is, the ARM defines a valid probability distribution over finished responses of length at most TT. A proof is given in Appendix B.5.

To enforce the condition πq​(EOS|𝒔T)=1\pi_{q}(\texttt{EOS}|{\bm{s}}_{T})=1, we can define qq as in (11).

A.2 Handling variable-length sequences in EBMs

Probability of finished vs. unfinished responses.

Defining a probability over finished responses is more straightforward with EBMs, as we can directly parameterize ℙ⁡(Y=𝒚|X=𝒙){\mathbb{P}}(Y={\bm{y}}|X={\bm{x}}) for all possible 𝒚∈𝒴{\bm{y}}\in{\mathcal{Y}}. The negative energy RR of the EBM is, up to a constant factor, the log-probability of singletons events {Y=𝒚}\{Y={\bm{y}}\} given X=𝒙X={\bm{x}},

R⁡(𝒙,𝒚)=log⁡ℙ⁡(Y=𝒚|X=𝒙)+const⁡(𝒙).R({\bm{x}},{\bm{y}})=\log{\mathbb{P}}(Y={\bm{y}}|X={\bm{x}})+\mathrm{const}({\bm{x}}). (55)

Marginal probabilities ℙ⁡(Y≤τ=𝒚|X=𝒙){\mathbb{P}}(Y_{\leq\tau}={\bm{y}}|X={\bm{x}}) can be computed from ℙ⁡(Y=𝒚|X=𝒙){\mathbb{P}}(Y={\bm{y}}|X={\bm{x}}) by appropriate marginalization and similarly for the probability of response length.

Validity of the probability distribution over sequences.

An EBM defines a valid probability over finished responses of length up to TT by virtue of its normalization,

pREBM​(𝒚|𝒙)=exp⁡R⁡(𝒙,𝒚)∑𝒚′∈𝒴exp⁡R⁡(𝒙,𝒚′).p^{\text{EBM}}_{R}({\bm{y}}|{\bm{x}})=\frac{\exp R({\bm{x}},{\bm{y}})}{\sum_{{\bm{y}}^{\prime}\in{\mathcal{Y}}}\exp R({\bm{x}},{\bm{y}}^{\prime})}.

The denominator is well defined since 𝒴{\mathcal{Y}} is finite.

A.3 Chain rule of entropy

In this section, we show how the entropy of pp (the sequence distribution) can be computed in terms of the entropy of π\pi (the next-token distribution), using the law of total expectation (tower rule). This allows one to construct an unbiased estimator of the entropy of pp by sampling trajectories.

Stochastic state transition dynamics.


Suppose p⁡(𝝉|𝒔1)≔∏t=1Tπ⁡(at|st)​μ​(𝒔t+1|𝒔t,at)p({\bm{\tau}}|{\bm{s}}_{1})\coloneqq\prod_{t=1}^{T}\pi(a_{t}|s_{t})\mu({\bm{s}}_{t+1}|{\bm{s}}_{t},a_{t}) where 𝝉=(a1,s2,…,𝒔T,aT,sT+1){\bm{\tau}}=(a_{1},s_{2},\dots,{\bm{s}}_{T},a_{T},s_{T+1}). For all 𝒔1{\bm{s}}_{1}, we then have

H(p(⋅|𝒔1))\displaystyle H(p(\cdot|{\bm{s}}_{1})) =−𝔼τ∼p(⋅|𝒔1)[logp(τ|𝒔1)]\displaystyle=-{\mathbb{E}}_{\tau\sim p(\cdot|{\bm{s}}_{1})}\left[\log p(\tau|{\bm{s}}_{1})\right] (56)
=−𝔼τ∼p(⋅|𝒔1)[∑t=1Tlogπ(At|St)+logμ(St+1|St,At)]\displaystyle=-{\mathbb{E}}_{\tau\sim p(\cdot|{\bm{s}}_{1})}\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T}\log\pi(A_{t}|S_{t})+\log\mu(S_{t+1}|S_{t},A_{t})\right] (57)
=−∑t=1T𝔼St∼pt(⋅|𝒔1)[EAt∼π(⋅|St)[logπ(At|St)+𝔼St+1∼μ(⋅|St,At)[logμ(St+1|St,At)]]]\displaystyle=-\sum_{t=1}^{T}{\mathbb{E}}_{S_{t}\sim p_{t}(\cdot|{\bm{s}}_{1})}\left[E_{A_{t}\sim\pi(\cdot|S_{t})}\left[\log\pi(A_{t}|S_{t})+{\mathbb{E}}_{S_{t+1}\sim\mu(\cdot|S_{t},A_{t})}\left[\log\mu(S_{t+1}|S_{t},A_{t})\right]\right]\right] (58)
=∑t=1T𝔼St∼pt(⋅|𝒔1)[H(π(⋅|St))]+𝔼St∼pt(⋅|𝒔1),At∼π(⋅|St)[H(μ(⋅|St,At))]\displaystyle=\sum_{t=1}^{T}{\mathbb{E}}_{S_{t}\sim p_{t}(\cdot|{\bm{s}}_{1})}\left[H(\pi(\cdot|S_{t}))\right]+{\mathbb{E}}_{S_{t}\sim p_{t}(\cdot|{\bm{s}}_{1}),A_{t}\sim\pi(\cdot|S_{t})}\left[H(\mu(\cdot|S_{t},A_{t}))\right] (59)

where pt​(St|𝒔1)p_{t}(S_{t}|{\bm{s}}_{1}) is the marginal probability of being in state StS_{t} at time tt over all possible trajectories starting from 𝒔1{\bm{s}}_{1}.

Deterministic state transition dynamics.


Suppose p⁡(𝒚|𝒙)≔∏t=1Tπ⁡(yt|𝒙,𝒚<t)p({\bm{y}}|{\bm{x}})\coloneqq\prod_{t=1}^{T}\pi(y_{t}|{\bm{x}},{\bm{y}}_{<t}). For all 𝒙{\bm{x}}, we now have

H(p(⋅|𝒙))\displaystyle H(p(\cdot|{\bm{x}})) =−𝔼Y∼p(⋅|𝒙)[logp(Y|𝒙)]\displaystyle=-{\mathbb{E}}_{Y\sim p(\cdot|{\bm{x}})}\left[\log p(Y|{\bm{x}})\right] (60)
=−𝔼Y∼p(⋅|𝒙)[∑t=1Tlogπ(Yt|𝒙,Y<t)]\displaystyle=-{\mathbb{E}}_{Y\sim p(\cdot|{\bm{x}})}\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T}\log\pi(Y_{t}|{\bm{x}},Y_{<t})\right] (61)
=−∑t=1T𝔼Y<t∼ARπ(⋅|𝒙)[𝔼Yt∼π(⋅|𝒙,Y<t)[logπ(Yt|𝒙,Y<t)]]\displaystyle=-\sum_{t=1}^{T}{\mathbb{E}}_{Y_{<t}\overset{\text{AR}}{\sim}\pi(\cdot|{\bm{x}})}\left[{\mathbb{E}}_{Y_{t}\sim\pi(\cdot|{\bm{x}},Y_{<t})}\left[\log\pi(Y_{t}|{\bm{x}},Y_{<t})\right]\right] (62)
=∑t=1T𝔼Y<t∼ARπ(⋅|𝒙)[H(π(⋅|𝒙,Y<t))]\displaystyle=\sum_{t=1}^{T}{\mathbb{E}}_{Y_{<t}\overset{\text{AR}}{\sim}\pi(\cdot|{\bm{x}})}\left[H(\pi(\cdot|{\bm{x}},Y_{<t}))\right] (63)
=∑t=1TH⁡(Yt|𝒙,Y<t)\displaystyle=\sum_{t=1}^{T}H(Y_{t}|{\bm{x}},Y_{<t}) (64)

where we use ∼AR\overset{\text{AR}}{\sim} to indicate that Y<tY_{<t} is obtained autoregressively.

Taking the expectation over 𝒙{\bm{x}}, we obtain the conditional entropy

𝔼X[H(p(⋅|X))]=H(Y|X)=∑t=1TH(Yt|X,Y<t).{\mathbb{E}}_{X}\left[H(p(\cdot|X))\right]=H(Y|X)=\sum_{t=1}^{T}H(Y_{t}|X,Y_{<t}). (65)

A.4 Chain rule of Kullback-Leibler divergence

In this section, we show a similar result for the Kullback-Leibler divergence as for the entropy. This allows one to construct an unbiased estimator of the KL divergence by sampling trajectories.

Stochastic state transition dynamics.


Suppose p⁡(𝝉|𝒔1)≔∏t=1Tπ⁡(at|st)​μ​(𝒔t+1|𝒔t,at)p({\bm{\tau}}|{\bm{s}}_{1})\coloneqq\prod_{t=1}^{T}\pi(a_{t}|s_{t})\mu({\bm{s}}_{t+1}|{\bm{s}}_{t},a_{t}) and p0​(𝝉|𝒔1)≔∏t=1Tπ0​(at|st)​μ​(𝒔t+1|𝒔t,at)p_{0}({\bm{\tau}}|{\bm{s}}_{1})\coloneqq\prod_{t=1}^{T}\pi_{0}(a_{t}|s_{t})\mu({\bm{s}}_{t+1}|{\bm{s}}_{t},a_{t}) where 𝝉=(a1,𝒔2,…,𝒔T,aT,𝒔T+1){\bm{\tau}}=(a_{1},{\bm{s}}_{2},\dots,{\bm{s}}_{T},a_{T},{\bm{s}}_{T+1}). For all 𝒔1{\bm{s}}_{1}, we have

KL(p(⋅|𝒔1),p0(⋅|𝒔1))\displaystyle\mathrm{KL}(p(\cdot|{\bm{s}}_{1}),p_{0}(\cdot|{\bm{s}}_{1})) =𝔼τ∼p(⋅|𝒔1)[logp⁡(τ|𝒔1)p0​(τ|𝒔1)]\displaystyle={\mathbb{E}}_{\tau\sim p(\cdot|{\bm{s}}_{1})}\left[\log\frac{p(\tau|{\bm{s}}_{1})}{p_{0}(\tau|{\bm{s}}_{1})}\right] (66)
=𝔼τ∼p(⋅|𝒔1)[∑t=1Tlogπ⁡(At|St)​μ​(St+1|St,At)π0​(At|St)​μ​(St+1|St,At)]\displaystyle={\mathbb{E}}_{\tau\sim p(\cdot|{\bm{s}}_{1})}\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T}\log\frac{\pi(A_{t}|S_{t})\mu(S_{t+1}|S_{t},A_{t})}{\pi_{0}(A_{t}|S_{t})\mu(S_{t+1}|S_{t},A_{t})}\right] (67)
=∑t=1T𝔼St∼pt(⋅|𝒔1)[𝔼At∼π(⋅|St)[logπ⁡(At|St)π0​(At|St)]]\displaystyle=\sum_{t=1}^{T}{\mathbb{E}}_{S_{t}\sim p_{t}(\cdot|{\bm{s}}_{1})}\left[{\mathbb{E}}_{A_{t}\sim\pi(\cdot|S_{t})}\left[\log\frac{\pi(A_{t}|S_{t})}{\pi_{0}(A_{t}|S_{t})}\right]\right] (68)
=∑t=1T𝔼St∼pt(⋅|𝒔1)[KL(π(⋅|St),π0(⋅|St))],\displaystyle=\sum_{t=1}^{T}{\mathbb{E}}_{S_{t}\sim p_{t}(\cdot|{\bm{s}}_{1})}\left[\mathrm{KL}(\pi(\cdot|S_{t}),\pi_{0}(\cdot|S_{t}))\right], (69)

where pt​(St|𝒔1)p_{t}(S_{t}|{\bm{s}}_{1}) is again the marginal probability of being in state StS_{t} at time tt over all possible trajectories starting from 𝒔1{\bm{s}}_{1}. We see that the state transition kernel μ\mu cancels out.

Deterministic state transition dynamics.


Similarly, suppose p⁡(𝒚|𝒙)≔∏t=1Tπ⁡(yt|𝒙,𝒚<t)p({\bm{y}}|{\bm{x}})\coloneqq\prod_{t=1}^{T}\pi(y_{t}|{\bm{x}},{\bm{y}}_{<t}) and p0​(𝒚|𝒙)≔∏t=1Tπ0​(yt|𝒙,𝒚<t)p_{0}({\bm{y}}|{\bm{x}})\coloneqq\prod_{t=1}^{T}\pi_{0}(y_{t}|{\bm{x}},{\bm{y}}_{<t}). For all 𝒙{\bm{x}}, we have

KL(p(⋅|𝒙),p0(⋅|𝒙))\displaystyle\mathrm{KL}(p(\cdot|{\bm{x}}),p_{0}(\cdot|{\bm{x}})) =𝔼Y∼p(⋅|𝒙)[logp⁡(Y|𝒙)p0​(Y|𝒙)]\displaystyle={\mathbb{E}}_{Y\sim p(\cdot|{\bm{x}})}\left[\log\frac{p(Y|{\bm{x}})}{p_{0}(Y|{\bm{x}})}\right] (70)
=𝔼Y∼p(⋅|𝒙)[∑t=1Tlogπ⁡(Yt|𝒙,Y<t)π0​(Yt|𝒙,Y<t)]\displaystyle={\mathbb{E}}_{Y\sim p(\cdot|{\bm{x}})}\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T}\log\frac{\pi(Y_{t}|{\bm{x}},Y_{<t})}{\pi_{0}(Y_{t}|{\bm{x}},Y_{<t})}\right] (71)
=∑t=1T𝔼Y<t∼ARπ(⋅|𝒙)[𝔼Yt∼π(⋅|𝒙,Y<t)[logπ⁡(Yt|𝒙,Y<t)π0​(Yt|𝒙,Y<t)]]\displaystyle=\sum_{t=1}^{T}{\mathbb{E}}_{Y_{<t}\overset{\text{AR}}{\sim}\pi(\cdot|{\bm{x}})}\left[{\mathbb{E}}_{Y_{t}\sim\pi(\cdot|{\bm{x}},Y_{<t})}\left[\log\frac{\pi(Y_{t}|{\bm{x}},Y_{<t})}{\pi_{0}(Y_{t}|{\bm{x}},Y_{<t})}\right]\right] (72)
=∑t=1T𝔼Y<t∼ARπ(⋅|𝒙)[KL(π(⋅|𝒙,Y<t),π0(⋅|𝒙,Y<t))]\displaystyle=\sum_{t=1}^{T}{\mathbb{E}}_{Y_{<t}\overset{\text{AR}}{\sim}\pi(\cdot|{\bm{x}})}\left[\mathrm{KL}(\pi(\cdot|{\bm{x}},Y_{<t}),\pi_{0}(\cdot|{\bm{x}},Y_{<t}))\right] (73)
≔∑t=1TKL⁡(π⁡(Yt|𝒙,Y<t),π0​(Yt|𝒙,Y<t))\displaystyle\coloneqq\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathrm{KL}(\pi(Y_{t}|{\bm{x}},Y_{<t}),\pi_{0}(Y_{t}|{\bm{x}},Y_{<t})) (74)

where we again use ∼AR\overset{\text{AR}}{\sim} to indicate that Y<tY_{<t} is obtained autoregressively.

Taking the expectation over 𝒙{\bm{x}}, we obtain the conditional Kullback-Leibler divergence

𝔼X[KL(p(⋅|X),p0(⋅|X))]=KL(p(Y|X),p0(Y|X))=∑t=1TKL(π(Yt|X,Y<t),π0(Yt|X,Y<t)).{\mathbb{E}}_{X}\left[\mathrm{KL}(p(\cdot|X),p_{0}(\cdot|X))\right]=\mathrm{KL}(p(Y|X),p_{0}(Y|X))=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathrm{KL}(\pi(Y_{t}|X,Y_{<t}),\pi_{0}(Y_{t}|X,Y_{<t})). (75)

Estimators based on Rao–Blackwellization are studied in (Amini et al., 2025).

A.5 Bijection with a reference measure

Suppose we have a reference distribution

pref​(𝒚|𝒙)≔∏t=1|𝒚|πref​(yt|𝒙⊕𝒚<t).p_{\mathrm{ref}}({\bm{y}}|{\bm{x}})\coloneqq\prod_{t=1}^{|{\bm{y}}|}\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_{t}|{\bm{x}}\oplus{\bm{y}}_{<t}). (76)

We then have

Rref​(𝒙,𝒚)=log⁡pref​(𝒚|𝒙)=∑t=1|𝒚|log⁡πref​(yt|𝒙⊕𝒚<t)=∑t=1|𝒚|qref​(𝒙⊕𝒚<t,yt),R_{\mathrm{ref}}({\bm{x}},{\bm{y}})=\log p_{\mathrm{ref}}({\bm{y}}|{\bm{x}})=\sum_{t=1}^{|{\bm{y}}|}\log\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_{t}|{\bm{x}}\oplus{\bm{y}}_{<t})=\sum_{t=1}^{|{\bm{y}}|}q_{\mathrm{ref}}({\bm{x}}\oplus{\bm{y}}_{<t},y_{t}), (77)

where qref​(𝒔,y)≔log⁡πref​(y|𝒔)q_{\mathrm{ref}}({\bm{s}},y)\coloneqq\log\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y|{\bm{s}}). Suppose further that

R⁡(𝒙,𝒚)≔∑t=1|𝒚|r⁡(𝒙⊕𝒚<t,yt).\displaystyle R({\bm{x}},{\bm{y}})\coloneqq\sum_{t=1}^{|{\bm{y}}|}r({\bm{x}}\oplus{\bm{y}}_{<t},y_{t}). (78)

Using the bijection for the total energy R′≔R+RrefR^{\prime}\coloneqq R+R_{\mathrm{ref}}, we obtain the total logits q′q^{\prime},

q′​(𝒔t,yt)≔{r⁡(𝒔t,yt)+qref​(𝒔t,yt)if​yt=EOSr⁡(𝒔t,yt)+qref​(𝒔t,yt)+Vq′​(𝒔t⊕yt)if​yt≠EOS.q^{\prime}({\bm{s}}_{t},y_{t})\coloneqq\begin{cases}r({\bm{s}}_{t},y_{t})+q_{\mathrm{ref}}({\bm{s}}_{t},y_{t})&\mbox{if}~y_{t}=\texttt{EOS}\\ r({\bm{s}}_{t},y_{t})+q_{\mathrm{ref}}({\bm{s}}_{t},y_{t})+V_{q^{\prime}}({\bm{s}}_{t}\oplus y_{t})&\mbox{if}~y_{t}\neq\texttt{EOS}\end{cases}. (79)

We now define the residual logits qq such that q′≔q+qrefq^{\prime}\coloneqq q+q_{\mathrm{ref}}, which implies

πq′​(yt|𝒔t)∝πref​(yt|𝒔t)​exp⁡(q⁡(𝒔t,yt)).\pi_{q^{\prime}}(y_{t}|{\bm{s}}_{t})\propto\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_{t}|{\bm{s}}_{t})\exp(q({\bm{s}}_{t},y_{t})). (80)

Substituting q′=q+qrefq^{\prime}=q+q_{\mathrm{ref}} into the recursion above, the term qrefq_{\mathrm{ref}} cancels out on both sides. The mapping between rr and qq is therefore

q⁡(𝒔t,yt)≔{r⁡(𝒔t,yt)if​yt=EOSr⁡(𝒔t,yt)+Vq+qref​(𝒔t⊕yt)if​yt≠EOS,q({\bm{s}}_{t},y_{t})\coloneqq\begin{cases}r({\bm{s}}_{t},y_{t})&\mbox{if}~y_{t}=\texttt{EOS}\\ r({\bm{s}}_{t},y_{t})+V_{q+q_{\mathrm{ref}}}({\bm{s}}_{t}\oplus y_{t})&\mbox{if}~y_{t}\neq\texttt{EOS}\end{cases}, (81)

where

Vq+qref(𝒔t)=log𝔼Yt∼πref(⋅|𝒔t)[exp(q(𝒔t,Yt))],V_{q+q_{\mathrm{ref}}}({\bm{s}}_{t})=\log{\mathbb{E}}_{Y_{t}\sim\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(\cdot|{\bm{s}}_{t})}[\exp(q({\bm{s}}_{t},Y_{t}))], (82)

which is the log-sum-exp modulated by the reference measure.

A.6 Chain rule of probability perspective on the bijection

In this section, we revisit Proposition 3.2 from a chain rule of probability perspective, by using the algorithm outlined in Section 3.1. We use a fixed length TT for simplicity of the exposition. We have

p⁡(𝒚|𝒙)\displaystyle p({\bm{y}}|{\bm{x}}) =exp⁡(r⁡(𝒔1,y1)+⋯+r⁡(𝒔T,yT))Z⁡(𝒙)\displaystyle=\frac{\exp(r({\bm{s}}_{1},y_{1})+\dots+r({\bm{s}}_{T},y_{T}))}{Z({\bm{x}})} (83)
=exp⁡(r⁡(𝒔1,y1)+⋯+r⁡(𝒔T−1,yT−1))​exp⁡(r⁡(𝒔T,yT))Z⁡(𝒙)\displaystyle=\frac{\exp(r({\bm{s}}_{1},y_{1})+\dots+r({\bm{s}}_{T-1},y_{T-1}))\exp(r({\bm{s}}_{T},y_{T}))}{Z({\bm{x}})} (84)

where Z⁡(𝒙)Z({\bm{x}}) is the normalization constant.

Marginalizing the last variable, we obtain

p⁡(𝒚≤T−1|𝒙)\displaystyle p({\bm{y}}_{\leq T-1}|{\bm{x}}) =∑yT∈𝒱p⁡(𝒚<T,yT|𝒙)\displaystyle=\sum_{y_{T}\in{\mathcal{V}}}p({\bm{y}}_{<T},y_{T}|{\bm{x}}) (85)
=1Z⁡(𝒙)​exp⁡(r⁡(𝒔1,y1)+⋯+r⁡(𝒔T−1,yT−1))​∑yT∈𝒱exp⁡(r⁡(𝒔T,yT))\displaystyle=\frac{1}{Z({\bm{x}})}\exp(r({\bm{s}}_{1},y_{1})+\dots+r({\bm{s}}_{T-1},y_{T-1}))\sum_{y_{T}\in{\mathcal{V}}}\exp(r({\bm{s}}_{T},y_{T})) (86)
=1Z⁡(𝒙)​exp⁡(r⁡(𝒔1,y1)+⋯+r⁡(𝒔T−1,yT−1))​exp⁡(Vr​(𝒔T)).\displaystyle=\frac{1}{Z({\bm{x}})}\exp(r({\bm{s}}_{1},y_{1})+\dots+r({\bm{s}}_{T-1},y_{T-1}))\exp(V_{r}({\bm{s}}_{T})). (87)

By conditioning, we obtain

π⁡(yT|𝒙,𝒚<T)\displaystyle\pi(y_{T}|{\bm{x}},{\bm{y}}_{<T}) =p⁡(𝒚≤T|𝒙)p⁡(𝒚≤T−1|𝒙)\displaystyle=\frac{p({\bm{y}}_{\leq T}|{\bm{x}})}{p({\bm{y}}_{\leq T-1}|{\bm{x}})} (88)
=exp⁡(r⁡(𝒔T,yT)−Vr​(𝒔T))\displaystyle=\exp(r({\bm{s}}_{T},y_{T})-V_{r}({\bm{s}}_{T})) (89)
=exp⁡(q⁡(𝒔T,yT)−Vq​(𝒔T))\displaystyle=\exp(q({\bm{s}}_{T},y_{T})-V_{q}({\bm{s}}_{T})) (90)

where we have used that p⁡(𝒚|𝒙)=p⁡(𝒚≤T|𝒙)p({\bm{y}}|{\bm{x}})=p({\bm{y}}_{\leq T}|{\bm{x}}) and where we defined q⁡(𝒔T,yT)≔r⁡(𝒔T,yT)q({\bm{s}}_{T},y_{T})\coloneqq r({\bm{s}}_{T},y_{T}).

Marginalizing once again, we obtain

p⁡(𝒚≤T−2|𝒙)\displaystyle p({\bm{y}}_{\leq T-2}|{\bm{x}}) =∑yT−1∈𝒱p⁡(𝒚<T−1,yT−1|𝒙)\displaystyle=\sum_{y_{T-1}\in{\mathcal{V}}}p({\bm{y}}_{<T-1},y_{T-1}|{\bm{x}}) (91)
=1Z⁡(𝒙)​exp⁡(r⁡(𝒔1,y1)+⋯+r⁡(𝒔T−2,yT−2))​∑yT−1∈𝒱exp⁡(r⁡(𝒔T−1,yT−1)+Vq​(𝒔T−1⊕yT−1))\displaystyle=\frac{1}{Z({\bm{x}})}\exp(r({\bm{s}}_{1},y_{1})+\dots+r({\bm{s}}_{T-2},y_{T-2}))\sum_{y_{T-1}\in{\mathcal{V}}}\exp(r({\bm{s}}_{T-1},y_{T-1})+V_{q}({\bm{s}}_{T-1}\oplus y_{T-1})) (92)
=1Z⁡(𝒙)​exp⁡(r⁡(𝒔1,y1)+⋯+r⁡(𝒔T−2,yT−2))​exp⁡(Vq​(𝒔T−1)),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{Z({\bm{x}})}\exp(r({\bm{s}}_{1},y_{1})+\dots+r({\bm{s}}_{T-2},y_{T-2}))\exp(V_{q}({\bm{s}}_{T-1})), (93)

where we defined q⁡(𝒔T−1,yT−1)≔r⁡(𝒔T−1,yT−1)+Vq​(𝒔T−1⊕yT−1⏟𝒔T)q({\bm{s}}_{T-1},y_{T-1})\coloneqq r({\bm{s}}_{T-1},y_{T-1})+V_{q}(\underbrace{{\bm{s}}_{T-1}\oplus y_{T-1}}_{{\bm{s}}_{T}}).

By conditioning once again, we obtain

π⁡(yT−1|𝒙,𝒚<T−1)\displaystyle\pi(y_{T-1}|{\bm{x}},{\bm{y}}_{<T-1}) =p⁡(𝒚≤T−1|𝒙)p⁡(𝒚≤T−2|𝒙)\displaystyle=\frac{p({\bm{y}}_{\leq T-1}|{\bm{x}})}{p({\bm{y}}_{\leq T-2}|{\bm{x}})} (94)
=exp⁡(q⁡(𝒔T−1,yT−1)−Vq​(𝒔T−1)).\displaystyle=\exp(q({\bm{s}}_{T-1},y_{T-1})-V_{q}({\bm{s}}_{T-1})). (95)

Repeating the process until t=1t=1, we recover the mapping ℳ{\mathcal{M}}

q⁡(𝒔T,yT)\displaystyle q({\bm{s}}_{T},y_{T}) ≔r⁡(𝒔T,yT)\displaystyle\coloneqq r({\bm{s}}_{T},y_{T}) (96)
q⁡(𝒔T−1,yT−1)\displaystyle q({\bm{s}}_{T-1},y_{T-1}) ≔r⁡(𝒔T−1,yT−1)+Vq​(𝒔T)\displaystyle\coloneqq r({\bm{s}}_{T-1},y_{T-1})+V_{q}({\bm{s}}_{T}) (97)
⋮\displaystyle~~\vdots (98)
q⁡(𝒔1,y1)\displaystyle q({\bm{s}}_{1},y_{1}) ≔r⁡(𝒔1,y1)+Vq​(𝒔2).\displaystyle\coloneqq r({\bm{s}}_{1},y_{1})+V_{q}({\bm{s}}_{2}). (99)

A.7 Variational perspective on the bijection

In this section, we revisit Proposition 3.2 from a variational perspective. We use a fixed length TT for simplicity of the exposition. We notice that

ARrebm​(𝒙)\displaystyle A^{\textsc{ebm}}_{R_{r}}({\bm{x}}) (100)
=\displaystyle= maxp∈𝒫⁡(𝒴|𝒙)𝔼Y∼p(⋅|𝒙)[Rr(𝒙,Y)−logp(Y|𝒙)]\displaystyle\max_{p\in{\mathcal{P}}({\mathcal{Y}}|{\bm{x}})}{\mathbb{E}}_{Y\sim p(\cdot|{\bm{x}})}[R_{r}({\bm{x}},Y)-\log p(Y|{\bm{x}})] (101)
=\displaystyle= maxπ∈𝒫⁡(𝒱|𝒮⁡(𝒙))𝔼Y1∼π(⋅|𝒙)[r(𝒙,Y1)−logπ(Y1|𝒙)+⋯+𝔼YT∼π(⋅|𝒙⊕Y<T)[r(𝒙⊕Y<T,YT)−logπ(YT|𝒙⊕Y<T)]]\displaystyle\max_{\pi\in{\mathcal{P}}({\mathcal{V}}|{\mathcal{S}}({\bm{x}}))}{\mathbb{E}}_{Y_{1}\sim\pi(\cdot|{\bm{x}})}\left[r({\bm{x}},Y_{1})-\log\pi(Y_{1}|{\bm{x}})+\dots+{\mathbb{E}}_{Y_{T}\sim\pi(\cdot|{\bm{x}}\oplus Y_{<T})}[r({\bm{x}}\oplus Y_{<T},Y_{T})-\log\pi(Y_{T}|{\bm{x}}\oplus Y_{<T})]\right] (102)
=\displaystyle= maxOPENπ1∈𝒫⁡(𝒱|𝒮1​(𝒙)))πT∈𝒫⁡(𝒱|𝒮T−1​(𝒙))𝔼Y1∼π1(⋅|𝒙)[r(𝒙,Y1)−logπ1(Y1|𝒙)+⋯+𝔼YT∼πT(⋅|𝒙⊕Y<T)[r(𝒙⊕Y<T,YT)−logπT(YT|𝒙⊕Y<T)]]\displaystyle\max_{\begin{subarray}{c}\pi_{1}\in{\mathcal{P}}({\mathcal{V}}|{\mathcal{S}}_{1}({\bm{x}})))\\ \vdots\\ \pi_{T}\in{\mathcal{P}}({\mathcal{V}}|{\mathcal{S}}_{T-1}({\bm{x}}))\end{subarray}}{\mathbb{E}}_{Y_{1}\sim\pi_{1}(\cdot|{\bm{x}})}\left[r({\bm{x}},Y_{1})-\log\pi_{1}(Y_{1}|{\bm{x}})+\dots+{\mathbb{E}}_{Y_{T}\sim\pi_{T}(\cdot|{\bm{x}}\oplus Y_{<T})}[r({\bm{x}}\oplus Y_{<T},Y_{T})-\log\pi_{T}(Y_{T}|{\bm{x}}\oplus Y_{<T})]\right] (103)
=\displaystyle= maxπ1∈𝒫⁡(𝒱|𝒮1​(𝒙))𝔼Y1∼π1(⋅|𝒙)[r(𝒙,Y1)−logπ1(Y1|𝒙)+⋯+maxπT∈𝒫⁡(𝒱|𝒮T−1​(𝒙))𝔼YT∼πT(⋅|𝒙⊕Y<T)[r(𝒙⊕Y<T,YT)−logπT(YT|𝒙⊕Y<T)]].\displaystyle\max_{\pi_{1}\in{\mathcal{P}}({\mathcal{V}}|{\mathcal{S}}_{1}({\bm{x}}))}{\mathbb{E}}_{Y_{1}\sim\pi_{1}(\cdot|{\bm{x}})}\left[r({\bm{x}},Y_{1})-\log\pi_{1}(Y_{1}|{\bm{x}})+\dots+\max_{\pi_{T}\in{\mathcal{P}}({\mathcal{V}}|{\mathcal{S}}_{T-1}({\bm{x}}))}{\mathbb{E}}_{Y_{T}\sim\pi_{T}(\cdot|{\bm{x}}\oplus Y_{<T})}[r({\bm{x}}\oplus Y_{<T},Y_{T})-\log\pi_{T}(Y_{T}|{\bm{x}}\oplus Y_{<T})]\right]. (104)

Solving the nested maxima from right to left, it can indeed be checked that ARrebm​(𝒙)=Vq​(𝒙)A^{\textsc{ebm}}_{R_{r}}({\bm{x}})=V_{q}({\bm{x}}) for all 𝒙∈𝒳{\bm{x}}\in{\mathcal{X}} with q=ℳ⁡(r)q={\mathcal{M}}(r).

A.8 Adversarial and variational inference perspectives

We have for all R∈ℱ⁡(𝒳×𝒴)R\in{\mathcal{F}}({\mathcal{X}}\times{\mathcal{Y}}), 𝒙∈𝒳{\bm{x}}\in{\mathcal{X}} and 𝒚∈𝒴{\bm{y}}\in{\mathcal{Y}},

ARebm​(𝒙)\displaystyle A^{\textsc{ebm}}_{R}({\bm{x}}) =maxp∈𝒫⁡(𝒴|𝒙)𝔼Y∼p(⋅|𝒙)[R(𝒙,Y)−logp(Y|𝒙)]\displaystyle=\max_{p\in{\mathcal{P}}({\mathcal{Y}}|{\bm{x}})}{\mathbb{E}}_{Y\sim p(\cdot|{\bm{x}})}[R({\bm{x}},Y)-\log p(Y|{\bm{x}})] (105)
≥𝔼Y∼p(⋅|𝒙)[R(𝒙,Y)−logp(Y|𝒙)]∀p∈𝒫(𝒴|𝒙).\displaystyle\geq{\mathbb{E}}_{Y\sim p(\cdot|{\bm{x}})}[R({\bm{x}},Y)-\log p(Y|{\bm{x}})]\qquad\forall p\in{\mathcal{P}}({\mathcal{Y}}|{\bm{x}}). (106)

In the second line, equality holds when p=pRebmp=p^{\textsc{ebm}}_{R}.

From a convex duality perspective, RR is the primal variable and pp is the dual variable.

In particular, we have for all R∈ℱ⁡(𝒳×𝒴)R\in{\mathcal{F}}({\mathcal{X}}\times{\mathcal{Y}}), q∈ℱ⁡(𝒮×𝒜)q\in{\mathcal{F}}({\mathcal{S}}\times{\mathcal{A}}) and 𝒙∈𝒳{\bm{x}}\in{\mathcal{X}},

ARebm(𝒙)≥𝔼Y∼parmq(⋅|𝒙)[R(𝒙,Y)−logpqarm(Y|𝒙)]∀q∈ℱ(𝒮×𝒜).A^{\textsc{ebm}}_{R}({\bm{x}})\geq{\mathbb{E}}_{Y\sim p^{\textsc{arm}}_{q}(\cdot|{\bm{x}})}[R({\bm{x}},Y)-\log p^{\textsc{arm}}_{q}(Y|{\bm{x}})]\qquad\forall q\in{\mathcal{F}}({\mathcal{S}}\times{\mathcal{A}}). (107)

From Proposition 3.2, equality holds when q=ℳ⁡(r)q={\mathcal{M}}(r) and R=RrR=R_{r}.

We can use this perspective to derive a min-max formulation

minR∈ℱ⁡(𝒳×𝒴)𝔼(X,Y)[ℓRebm(X,Y)]=minR∈ℱ⁡(𝒳×𝒴)maxq∈ℱ⁡(𝒮×𝒜)𝔼X[𝔼Y′∼parmq(⋅|X)[R(X,Y′)−logpqarm(Y′|X)]]−𝔼(X,Y)[R(X,Y)].\min_{R\in{\mathcal{F}}({\mathcal{X}}\times{\mathcal{Y}})}{\mathbb{E}}_{(X,Y)}\left[\ell^{\textsc{ebm}}_{R}(X,Y)\right]=\min_{R\in{\mathcal{F}}({\mathcal{X}}\times{\mathcal{Y}})}\max_{q\in{\mathcal{F}}({\mathcal{S}}\times{\mathcal{A}})}{\mathbb{E}}_{X}\left[{\mathbb{E}}_{Y^{\prime}\sim p^{\textsc{arm}}_{q}(\cdot|X)}[R(X,Y^{\prime})-\log p^{\textsc{arm}}_{q}(Y^{\prime}|X)]\right]-{\mathbb{E}}_{(X,Y)}\left[R(X,Y)\right]. (108)

From a GAN or actor-critic perspective, pqarmp_{q}^{\textsc{arm}} is a generator (actor) and RR is a discriminator (critic).

From a variational inference perspective, ARebm​(𝒙)A^{\textsc{ebm}}_{R}({\bm{x}}) is the log-evidence and (q,R)↦𝔼Y∼pqarm​[R⁡(𝒙,Y)−log⁡pqarm​(Y|𝒙)](q,R)\mapsto{\mathbb{E}}_{Y\sim p^{\textsc{arm}}_{q}}[R({\bm{x}},Y)-\log p^{\textsc{arm}}_{q}(Y|{\bm{x}})] is known as the evidence lower-bound (ELBO). While it is a direct consequence of convex duality, the ELBO can also be derived using Jensen’s inequality or using the non-negativity of the KL. The distribution pqarmp^{\textsc{arm}}_{q} is the proposal distribution (easy to sample from) and the distribution pRebmp^{\textsc{ebm}}_{R} is the target distribution (difficult to sample from).

A.9 Probabilistic inference perspective

In this section, we revisit the bijection from a probabilistic inference perspective. Our exposition differs from (Levine, 2018) and may therefore bring a complementary view. Throughout the section, we define the shorthand notation 𝒔1≔𝒙{\bm{s}}_{1}\coloneqq{\bm{x}} and 𝒔t≔𝒙⊕𝒚<t{\bm{s}}_{t}\coloneqq{\bm{x}}\oplus{\bm{y}}_{<t} for t>1t>1.

The conditional probability of 𝒚{\bm{y}} given 𝒙{\bm{x}} according to an EBM is

p⁡(𝒚|𝒙)=1Z⁡(𝒙)​∏t=1Tψ⁡(𝒔t,yt),p({\bm{y}}|{\bm{x}})=\frac{1}{Z({\bm{x}})}\prod_{t=1}^{T}\psi({\bm{s}}_{t},y_{t}), (109)

where we defined the potential ψ⁡(𝒔t,yt)≔exp⁡(r⁡(𝒔t,yt))\psi({\bm{s}}_{t},y_{t})\coloneqq\exp(r({\bm{s}}_{t},y_{t})).

The partition function is defined as

Z⁡(𝒙)≔∑𝒚∈𝒴∏t=1Tψ⁡(𝒔t,yt).Z({\bm{x}})\coloneqq\sum_{{\bm{y}}\in{\mathcal{Y}}}\prod_{t=1}^{T}\psi({\bm{s}}_{t},y_{t}). (110)

Using the distributivity of multiplication over addition, we can expand Z⁡(𝒙)Z({\bm{x}}) as

Z⁡(𝒙)=∑y1∈𝒜ψ⁡(𝒔1,y1)​∑y2∈𝒜ψ⁡(𝒔2,y2)​…​∑yT∈𝒜ψ⁡(𝒔T,yT).Z({\bm{x}})=\sum_{y_{1}\in{\mathcal{A}}}\psi({\bm{s}}_{1},y_{1})\sum_{y_{2}\in{\mathcal{A}}}\psi({\bm{s}}_{2},y_{2})\dots\sum_{y_{T}\in{\mathcal{A}}}\psi({\bm{s}}_{T},y_{T}). (111)

Forward and backward variables.

Let us define the forward variables as

α1​(𝒔1)\displaystyle\alpha_{1}({\bm{s}}_{1}) ≔1\displaystyle\coloneqq 1 (112)
αt​(𝒔t)\displaystyle\alpha_{t}({\bm{s}}_{t}) ≔ψ⁡(𝒔1,y1)​…​ψ​(𝒔t−1,yt−1)∀t>1\displaystyle\coloneqq\psi({\bm{s}}_{1},y_{1})\dots\psi({\bm{s}}_{t-1},y_{t-1})\qquad\forall t>1 (113)
=αt−1​(𝒔t−1)​ψ​(𝒔t−1,yt−1).\displaystyle=\alpha_{t-1}({\bm{s}}_{t-1})\psi({\bm{s}}_{t-1},y_{t-1}). (114)

They capture the accumulated value of a single specific path from the root to the current state 𝒔t{\bm{s}}_{t} (the past).

Likewise, let us define the backward variables as

βt​(𝒔t)\displaystyle\beta_{t}({\bm{s}}_{t}) ≔∑yt∈𝒜ψ⁡(𝒔t,yt)​…​∑yT∈𝒜ψ⁡(𝒔T,yT)∀t≤T\displaystyle\coloneqq\sum_{y_{t}\in{\mathcal{A}}}\psi({\bm{s}}_{t},y_{t})\dots\sum_{y_{T}\in{\mathcal{A}}}\psi({\bm{s}}_{T},y_{T})\qquad\forall t\leq T (115)
=∑yt∈𝒜ψ⁡(𝒔t,yt)​βt+1​(𝒔t⊕yt)\displaystyle=\sum_{y_{t}\in{\mathcal{A}}}\psi({\bm{s}}_{t},y_{t})\beta_{t+1}({\bm{s}}_{t}\oplus y_{t}) (116)
βT+1​(⋅)\displaystyle\beta_{T+1}(\cdot) ≔1.\displaystyle\coloneqq 1. (117)

They capture the future value of being in state 𝒔t{\bm{s}}_{t}.

We then have for all t∈[T]t\in[T]

Z⁡(𝒙)=∑𝒔t∈𝒮t​(𝒙)αt​(𝒔t)​βt​(𝒔t),Z({\bm{x}})=\sum_{{\bm{s}}_{t}\in{\mathcal{S}}_{t}({\bm{x}})}\alpha_{t}({\bm{s}}_{t})\beta_{t}({\bm{s}}_{t}), (118)

where 𝒮t​(𝒙){\mathcal{S}}_{t}({\bm{x}}) is the set of all responses 𝒚{\bm{y}} of length t−1t-1 starting from 𝒔1=𝒙{\bm{s}}_{1}={\bm{x}} (i.e., nodes at depth t−1t-1 in the tree).

In particular:

  • •

    At the root (t=1t=1), the sum collapses to a single term, Z⁡(𝒙)=α1​(𝒙)​β1​(𝒙)=β1​(𝒙)Z({\bm{x}})=\alpha_{1}({\bm{x}})\beta_{1}({\bm{x}})=\beta_{1}({\bm{x}}).

  • •

    At the last step (t=Tt=T), the sum becomes Z⁡(𝒙)=∑𝒔T∈𝒮T​(𝒙)αT​(𝒔T)​βT​(𝒔T)Z({\bm{x}})=\sum_{{\bm{s}}_{T}\in{\mathcal{S}}_{T}({\bm{x}})}\alpha_{T}({\bm{s}}_{T})\beta_{T}({\bm{s}}_{T}).

Relationship with the bijection.

We can recover the relationship between EBMs and ARMs when examining the recursive definition of βt\beta_{t}. Dividing (116) by βt​(𝒔t)\beta_{t}({\bm{s}}_{t}) on both sides, we obtain

∑yt∈𝒜ψ⁡(𝒔t,yt)​βt+1​(𝒔t⊕yt)βt​(𝒔t)=1.\sum_{y_{t}\in{\mathcal{A}}}\frac{\psi({\bm{s}}_{t},y_{t})\beta_{t+1}({\bm{s}}_{t}\oplus y_{t})}{\beta_{t}({\bm{s}}_{t})}=1. (119)

Since the terms in the sum are positive and sum to 1, they define a valid probability distribution over the next token yty_{t}. This distribution is exactly πq\pi_{q}. To see why, recall that

πq​(yt|𝒔t)=exp⁡(q⁡(𝒔t,yt)−Vq​(𝒔t)).\pi_{q}(y_{t}|{\bm{s}}_{t})=\exp(q({\bm{s}}_{t},y_{t})-V_{q}({\bm{s}}_{t})). (120)

By identifying the terms, we find that

Vq​(𝒔t)\displaystyle V_{q}({\bm{s}}_{t}) =log⁡βt​(𝒔t)\displaystyle=\log\beta_{t}({\bm{s}}_{t}) (121)
q⁡(𝒔t,yt)\displaystyle q({\bm{s}}_{t},y_{t}) =log⁡ψ⁡(𝒔t,yt)+log⁡βt+1​(𝒔t⊕yt)\displaystyle=\log\psi({\bm{s}}_{t},y_{t})+\log\beta_{t+1}({\bm{s}}_{t}\oplus y_{t}) (122)
=r⁡(𝒔t,yt)+Vq​(𝒔t⊕yt).\displaystyle=r({\bm{s}}_{t},y_{t})+V_{q}({\bm{s}}_{t}\oplus y_{t}). (123)

We thus recover exactly the mapping q=ℳ⁡(r)q={\mathcal{M}}(r) presented in (21).

Furthermore, we can express the joint probability of a sequence 𝒚{\bm{y}} using the forward and backward variables. Substituting the expression for the policy derived above into the chain rule, we obtain

pqarm​(𝒚|𝒙)\displaystyle p^{\textsc{arm}}_{q}({\bm{y}}|{\bm{x}}) =∏t=1Tψ⁡(𝒔t,yt)​βt+1​(𝒔t+1)βt​(𝒔t)\displaystyle=\prod_{t=1}^{T}\frac{\psi({\bm{s}}_{t},y_{t})\beta_{t+1}({\bm{s}}_{t+1})}{\beta_{t}({\bm{s}}_{t})} (124)
=(∏t=1Tψ⁡(𝒔t,yt))​∏t=1Tβt+1​(𝒔t+1)βt​(𝒔t)⏟telescoping product\displaystyle=\left(\prod_{t=1}^{T}\psi({\bm{s}}_{t},y_{t})\right)\underbrace{\prod_{t=1}^{T}\frac{\beta_{t+1}({\bm{s}}_{t+1})}{\beta_{t}({\bm{s}}_{t})}}_{\text{telescoping product}} (125)
=(∏t=1Tψ⁡(𝒔t,yt))​βT+1​(𝒔T+1)β1​(𝒔1).\displaystyle=\left(\prod_{t=1}^{T}\psi({\bm{s}}_{t},y_{t})\right)\frac{\beta_{T+1}({\bm{s}}_{T+1})}{\beta_{1}({\bm{s}}_{1})}. (126)

Using the boundary conditions βT+1​(𝒔T+1)=1\beta_{T+1}({\bm{s}}_{T+1})=1 and β1​(𝒔1)=Z⁡(𝒙)\beta_{1}({\bm{s}}_{1})=Z({\bm{x}}), we recover exactly the definition of the EBM

pqarm​(𝒚|𝒙)\displaystyle p^{\textsc{arm}}_{q}({\bm{y}}|{\bm{x}}) =1Z⁡(𝒙)​∏t=1Tψ⁡(𝒔t,yt)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{Z({\bm{x}})}\prod_{t=1}^{T}\psi({\bm{s}}_{t},y_{t}) (127)
=pRrebm​(𝒚|𝒙).\displaystyle=p^{\textsc{ebm}}_{R_{r}}({\bm{y}}|{\bm{x}}). (128)

Irrelevance of forward variables for sampling.

While the forward variable αt​(𝒔t)\alpha_{t}({\bm{s}}_{t}) is essential for computing the edge marginals μq​(𝒔,y)\mu_{q}({\bm{s}},y), it is notably absent from the autoregressive generation process. The optimal policy πq​(yt|𝒔t)\pi_{q}(y_{t}|{\bm{s}}_{t}) represents the conditional probability of choosing yty_{t} given the current context 𝒔t{\bm{s}}_{t}. Using the forward-backward decomposition of the joint probability, we have

πq​(yt|𝒔t)=ℙ⁡(path through ​𝒔t⊕yt)ℙ⁡(path through ​𝒔t)=αt+1​(𝒔t⊕yt)​βt+1​(𝒔t⊕yt)αt​(𝒔t)​βt​(𝒔t).\pi_{q}(y_{t}|{\bm{s}}_{t})=\frac{{\mathbb{P}}(\text{path through }{\bm{s}}_{t}\oplus y_{t})}{{\mathbb{P}}(\text{path through }{\bm{s}}_{t})}=\frac{\alpha_{t+1}({\bm{s}}_{t}\oplus y_{t})\beta_{t+1}({\bm{s}}_{t}\oplus y_{t})}{\alpha_{t}({\bm{s}}_{t})\beta_{t}({\bm{s}}_{t})}. (129)

Substituting the recursive definition αt+1​(𝒔t⊕yt)=αt​(𝒔t)​ψ​(𝒔t,yt)\alpha_{t+1}({\bm{s}}_{t}\oplus y_{t})=\alpha_{t}({\bm{s}}_{t})\psi({\bm{s}}_{t},y_{t}), we observe that the forward variable cancels out

πq​(yt|𝒔t)=[αt​(𝒔t)​ψ​(𝒔t,yt)]​βt+1​(𝒔t⊕yt)αt​(𝒔t)​βt​(𝒔t)=ψ⁡(𝒔t,yt)​βt+1​(𝒔t⊕yt)βt​(𝒔t).\pi_{q}(y_{t}|{\bm{s}}_{t})=\frac{[\alpha_{t}({\bm{s}}_{t})\psi({\bm{s}}_{t},y_{t})]\beta_{t+1}({\bm{s}}_{t}\oplus y_{t})}{\alpha_{t}({\bm{s}}_{t})\beta_{t}({\bm{s}}_{t})}=\frac{\psi({\bm{s}}_{t},y_{t})\beta_{t+1}({\bm{s}}_{t}\oplus y_{t})}{\beta_{t}({\bm{s}}_{t})}. (130)

Intuitively, since the decision at time tt is conditioned on the fixed history 𝒔t{\bm{s}}_{t}, the accumulated reward of that history (αt\alpha_{t}) is a constant scaling factor that applies equally to all possible next actions, and thus does not affect the relative probabilities. The policy depends exclusively on the immediate reward ψ\psi and the future value β\beta.

Difference with HMMs and CRFs.

It is instructive to contrast this formulation with standard hidden Markov models (HMMs) or linear-chain conditional random fields (CRFs). In those models, the transition graph forms a lattice or trellis where multiple distinct paths merge into the same state due to the Markov property. Consequently, the standard forward variable αt​(𝒔t)\alpha_{t}({\bm{s}}_{t}) represents a marginal quantity obtained by summing over all incoming paths. If we use a context size of 11 (as in bigram HMMs), the cost of the forward-backward algorithm is O⁡(T​V2)O(TV^{2}).

In contrast, we define the state of an ARM as the unique context 𝒔t≔𝒙⊕𝒚<t{\bm{s}}_{t}\coloneqq{\bm{x}}\oplus{\bm{y}}_{<t}. The underlying topology is therefore a prefix tree (or trie), where every node has exactly one parent (except the end node, which can have several parents). As a result, there is a unique path from 𝒔1=𝒙{\bm{s}}_{1}={\bm{x}} to 𝒔t{\bm{s}}_{t} and the summation over paths typically found in the forward recursion collapses to a single product term: there is no summation in (114). The cost of dynamic programming (the algorithm is backward only) is however O⁡(VT)O(V^{T}).

Strictly speaking, if the ARM has a fixed context window WW and the sequence length TT exceeds WW, the model becomes an order-WW Markov chain and the graph becomes a De Bruijn lattice. However, in most modern LLM settings, the context window is sufficiently large (W≫TW\gg T) that the non-merging tree topology is the relevant abstraction. If we use a context size of WW (as in nn-gram HMMs), the cost of forward-backward is O⁡(T​VW+1)O(TV^{W+1}).

A.10 Gradient maps

Energy-based models.

The gradient of the log-partition w.r.t. RR, known as the link function, is defined for all 𝒙∈𝒳{\bm{x}}\in{\mathcal{X}} as

∇RARebm​(𝒙)=g∈ℱ⁡(𝒳×𝒴)\nabla_{R}A^{\textsc{ebm}}_{R}({\bm{x}})=g\in{\mathcal{F}}({\mathcal{X}}\times{\mathcal{Y}}) (131)

where

g⁡(𝒙′,𝒚)≔{pRebm​(𝒚|𝒙)if​𝒙′=𝒙0otherwise.g({\bm{x}}^{\prime},{\bm{y}})\coloneqq\begin{cases}p^{\textsc{ebm}}_{R}({\bm{y}}|{\bm{x}})&\text{if}\ {\bm{x}}^{\prime}={\bm{x}}\\ 0&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}. (132)

Autoregressive models.

By analogy, the gradient w.r.t. qq of the “log-partition” along the sequence 𝒚{\bm{y}} given 𝒙{\bm{x}} is

∇qAqarm​(𝒙,𝒚)=g∈ℱ⁡(𝒮×𝒜),\nabla_{q}A^{\textsc{arm}}_{q}({\bm{x}},{\bm{y}})=g\in{\mathcal{F}}({\mathcal{S}}\times{\mathcal{A}}), (133)

where

g⁡(𝒔t′,⋅)≔{πq(⋅|𝒔t)if​𝒔t′=𝒔t0otherwiseg({\bm{s}}_{t}^{\prime},\cdot)\coloneqq\begin{cases}\pi_{q}(\cdot|{\bm{s}}_{t})&\text{if}\ {\bm{s}}_{t}^{\prime}={\bm{s}}_{t}\\ 0&\text{otherwise}\end{cases} (134)

and where 𝒔t≔𝒙⊕𝒚<t{\bm{s}}_{t}\coloneqq{\bm{x}}\oplus{\bm{y}}_{<t}. Critically, this gradient map depends on the specific sequence 𝒚{\bm{y}}, and the states 𝒔t{\bm{s}}_{t} it induces. This highlights a fundamental geometric difference: EBMs are defined by global normalization, while ARMs are defined by local normalization along a path.

A.11 Backpropagation

In this section, we derive backpropagation through Vq​(𝒙)V_{q}({\bm{x}}) following Mensch & Blondel (2018).

Bottom-up approach.

Defining Vq​(𝒔T+1)≔0V_{q}({\bm{s}}_{T+1})\coloneqq 0, we run the forward pass (value computation) from t=Tt=T to t=1t=1,

Vq​(𝒔t)=LSEyt∈𝒜​r​(𝒔t,yt)+Vq​(𝒔t⊕yt).V_{q}({\bm{s}}_{t})=\underset{y_{t}\in{\mathcal{A}}}{{\mathrm{LSE}}}~r({\bm{s}}_{t},y_{t})+V_{q}({\bm{s}}_{t}\oplus y_{t}). (135)

where qq is defined from rr as in (21). That is, after the forward pass is complete, we obtain q=ℳ⁡(r)q={\mathcal{M}}(r). Note that in Mensch & Blondel (2018), the topological order is from t=1t=1 to t=Tt=T because the numbering of nodes is opposite to our notation.

From the identity above, the local gradients are

∂Vq​(𝒔t)∂Vq​(𝒔t⊕yt)=∂Vq​(𝒔t)∂r⁡(𝒔t,yt)=πq​(yt|𝒔t).\frac{\partial V_{q}({\bm{s}}_{t})}{\partial V_{q}({\bm{s}}_{t}\oplus y_{t})}=\frac{\partial V_{q}({\bm{s}}_{t})}{\partial r({\bm{s}}_{t},y_{t})}=\pi_{q}(y_{t}|{\bm{s}}_{t}). (136)

Our goal is to compute the gradient of Vq​(𝒔1)=Vq​(𝒙)V_{q}({\bm{s}}_{1})=V_{q}({\bm{x}}) w.r.t. the reward rr (edge),

∇rVq​(𝒔1)=Gq∈ℱ⁡(𝒮×𝒜)\nabla_{r}V_{q}({\bm{s}}_{1})=G_{q}\in{\mathcal{F}}({\mathcal{S}}\times{\mathcal{A}}) (137)

where

Gq​(𝒔t,yt)≔∂Vq​(𝒔1)∂r⁡(𝒔t,yt).G_{q}({\bm{s}}_{t},y_{t})\coloneqq\frac{\partial V_{q}({\bm{s}}_{1})}{\partial r({\bm{s}}_{t},y_{t})}. (138)

For convenience, we also define the accumulated gradient at state (node) 𝒔t{\bm{s}}_{t},

δ⁡(𝒔t)≔∂Vq​(𝒔1)∂Vq​(𝒔t).\delta({\bm{s}}_{t})\coloneqq\frac{\partial V_{q}({\bm{s}}_{1})}{\partial V_{q}({\bm{s}}_{t})}. (139)

Since r⁡(𝒔t,yt)r({\bm{s}}_{t},y_{t}) influences only Vq​(𝒔t)V_{q}({\bm{s}}_{t}), we have

Gq​(𝒔t,yt)=∂Vq​(𝒔1)∂r⁡(𝒔t,yt)=∂Vq​(𝒔1)∂Vq​(𝒔t)​∂Vq​(𝒔t)∂r⁡(𝒔t,yt)=δ⁡(𝒔t)​πq​(yt|𝒔t).G_{q}({\bm{s}}_{t},y_{t})=\frac{\partial V_{q}({\bm{s}}_{1})}{\partial r({\bm{s}}_{t},y_{t})}=\frac{\partial V_{q}({\bm{s}}_{1})}{\partial V_{q}({\bm{s}}_{t})}\frac{\partial V_{q}({\bm{s}}_{t})}{\partial r({\bm{s}}_{t},y_{t})}=\delta({\bm{s}}_{t})\pi_{q}(y_{t}|{\bm{s}}_{t}). (140)

Similarly, thanks to the prefix tree structure of ARMs, there is only one path from 𝒔t{\bm{s}}_{t} to 𝒔t+1=𝒔t⊕yt{\bm{s}}_{t+1}={\bm{s}}_{t}\oplus y_{t}. As a result, Vq​(𝒔t⊕yt)V_{q}({\bm{s}}_{t}\oplus y_{t}) influences only Vq​(𝒔t)V_{q}({\bm{s}}_{t}) and we have

δ⁡(𝒔t+1)=∂Vq​(𝒔1)∂Vq​(𝒔t+1)=∂Vq​(𝒔1)∂Vq​(𝒔t)​∂Vq​(𝒔t)∂Vq​(𝒔t+1)=δ⁡(𝒔t)​πq​(yt|𝒔t).\delta({\bm{s}}_{t+1})=\frac{\partial V_{q}({\bm{s}}_{1})}{\partial V_{q}({\bm{s}}_{t+1})}=\frac{\partial V_{q}({\bm{s}}_{1})}{\partial V_{q}({\bm{s}}_{t})}\frac{\partial V_{q}({\bm{s}}_{t})}{\partial V_{q}({\bm{s}}_{t+1})}=\delta({\bm{s}}_{t})\pi_{q}(y_{t}|{\bm{s}}_{t}). (141)

Therefore, we have

Gq​(𝒔t,yt)=δ⁡(𝒔t)​πq​(yt|𝒔t)=δ⁡(𝒔t+1).G_{q}({\bm{s}}_{t},y_{t})=\delta({\bm{s}}_{t})\pi_{q}(y_{t}|{\bm{s}}_{t})=\delta({\bm{s}}_{t+1}). (142)

Defining δ⁡(𝒔1)≔1\delta({\bm{s}}_{1})\coloneqq 1, we can compute the backward pass from t=1t=1 to TT,

Gq​(𝒔t,yt)=δ⁡(𝒔t)​πq​(yt|𝒔t)=∏k=1tπq​(yk|𝒔k)=pqarm​(𝒚≤t|𝒙).G_{q}({\bm{s}}_{t},y_{t})=\delta({\bm{s}}_{t})\pi_{q}(y_{t}|{\bm{s}}_{t})=\prod_{k=1}^{t}\pi_{q}(y_{k}|{\bm{s}}_{k})=p^{\textsc{arm}}_{q}({\bm{y}}_{\leq t}|{\bm{x}}). (143)

This confirms that the gradient of the log-partition function Vq​(𝒔1)V_{q}({\bm{s}}_{1}) with respect to the local reward r⁡(𝒔t,yt)r({\bm{s}}_{t},y_{t}) for q=ℳ⁡(r)q={\mathcal{M}}(r) is exactly the marginal probability of the prefix 𝒚≤t{\bm{y}}_{\leq t} given 𝒙{\bm{x}}.

Connection with forward and backward variables.

Using the forward and backward variables from Section A.9, the gradient can be equivalently written as

Gq​(𝒔t,yt)\displaystyle G_{q}({\bm{s}}_{t},y_{t}) =∂Vq​(𝒔1)∂r⁡(𝒔t,yt)\displaystyle=\frac{\partial V_{q}({\bm{s}}_{1})}{\partial r({\bm{s}}_{t},y_{t})} (144)
=δ⁡(𝒔t)​πq​(yt|𝒔t)\displaystyle=\delta({\bm{s}}_{t})\pi_{q}(y_{t}|{\bm{s}}_{t}) (145)
=(αt​(𝒔t)​βt​(𝒔t)β1​(𝒔1))​(ψ⁡(𝒔t,yt)​βt+1​(𝒔t+1)βt​(𝒔t))\displaystyle=\left(\frac{\alpha_{t}({\bm{s}}_{t})\beta_{t}({\bm{s}}_{t})}{\beta_{1}({\bm{s}}_{1})}\right)\left(\frac{\psi({\bm{s}}_{t},y_{t})\beta_{t+1}({\bm{s}}_{t+1})}{\beta_{t}({\bm{s}}_{t})}\right) (146)
=αt+1​(𝒔t+1)​βt+1​(𝒔t+1)Z⁡(𝒙),\displaystyle=\frac{\alpha_{t+1}({\bm{s}}_{t+1})\beta_{t+1}({\bm{s}}_{t+1})}{Z({\bm{x}})}, (147)

where we used αt+1​(𝒔t+1)=αt​(𝒔t)​ψ​(𝒔t,yt)\alpha_{t+1}({\bm{s}}_{t+1})=\alpha_{t}({\bm{s}}_{t})\psi({\bm{s}}_{t},y_{t}) and β1​(𝒔1)=Z⁡(𝒙)\beta_{1}({\bm{s}}_{1})=Z({\bm{x}}).

{lemma}

[Stability of softargmax w.r.t. Kullback-Leibler divergence] For all f:[k]→ℝf\colon[k]\to{\mathbb{R}} and g:[k]→ℝg\colon[k]\to{\mathbb{R}}, we have

KL⁡(softargmax⁡(f),softargmax⁡(g))≤2​‖f−g‖∞{\mathrm{KL}}({\operatorname{softargmax}}(f),{\operatorname{softargmax}}(g))\leq 2\|f-g\|_{\infty} (148)

where ‖h‖∞≔maxj∈[k]⁡|h⁡(j)|\|h\|_{\infty}\coloneqq\max_{j\in[k]}|h(j)|.

Proof.

Let us define pf≔softargmax⁡(f)p_{f}\coloneqq{\operatorname{softargmax}}(f) and pg≔softargmax⁡(g)p_{g}\coloneqq{\operatorname{softargmax}}(g). We have

KL⁡(pf,pg)\displaystyle{\mathrm{KL}}(p_{f},p_{g}) =∑i∈[k]pf​(i)​log⁡pf​(i)pg​(i)\displaystyle=\sum_{i\in[k]}p_{f}(i)\log\frac{p_{f}(i)}{p_{g}(i)} (149)
=∑i∈[k]pf​(i)​((f⁡(i)−log⁡Zf)−(g⁡(i)−log⁡Zg))\displaystyle=\sum_{i\in[k]}p_{f}(i)((f(i)-\log Z_{f})-(g(i)-\log Z_{g})) (150)
=𝔼i∼pf​[f⁡(i)−g⁡(i)]−(log⁡Zf−log⁡Zg)\displaystyle={\mathbb{E}}_{i\sim p_{f}}[f(i)-g(i)]-(\log Z_{f}-\log Z_{g}) (151)

where Zf≔∑j∈[k]exp⁡(f⁡(j))Z_{f}\coloneqq\sum_{j\in[k]}\exp(f(j)) and Zg≔∑j∈[k]exp⁡(g⁡(j))Z_{g}\coloneqq\sum_{j\in[k]}\exp(g(j)).

Let us define ε≔‖f−g‖∞\varepsilon\coloneqq\|f-g\|_{\infty}.

Using f⁡(j)−g⁡(j)≤εf(j)-g(j)\leq\varepsilon for all j∈[k]j\in[k], we obtain

Zf\displaystyle Z_{f} =∑j∈[k]exp⁡(f⁡(j))\displaystyle=\sum_{j\in[k]}\exp(f(j)) (152)
=∑j∈[k]exp⁡(g⁡(j)+(f⁡(j)−g⁡(j)))\displaystyle=\sum_{j\in[k]}\exp(g(j)+(f(j)-g(j))) (153)
≤∑j∈[k]exp⁡(g⁡(j)+ε)\displaystyle\leq\sum_{j\in[k]}\exp(g(j)+\varepsilon) (154)
=exp⁡(ε)​∑j∈[k]exp⁡(g⁡(j))\displaystyle=\exp(\varepsilon)\sum_{j\in[k]}\exp(g(j)) (155)
=exp⁡(ε)​Zg\displaystyle=\exp(\varepsilon)Z_{g} (156)

and therefore

log⁡Zf≤log⁡Zg+ε.\log Z_{f}\leq\log Z_{g}+\varepsilon. (157)

Applying the same reasoning with g⁡(j)−f⁡(j)≤εg(j)-f(j)\leq\varepsilon for all j∈[k]j\in[k], we obtain

log⁡Zg≤log⁡Zf+ε.\log Z_{g}\leq\log Z_{f}+\varepsilon. (158)

Therefore, we obtain the tight bound

|log⁡Zf−log⁡Zg|≤ε.|\log Z_{f}-\log Z_{g}|\leq\varepsilon. (159)

We also have

𝔼i∼pf​[f⁡(i)−g⁡(i)]≤𝔼i∼pf​[ε]=ε.{\mathbb{E}}_{i\sim p_{f}}[f(i)-g(i)]\leq{\mathbb{E}}_{i\sim p_{f}}[\varepsilon]=\varepsilon. (160)

Overall, we therefore obtain

KL⁡(pf,pg)≤2​ε=2​‖f−g‖∞.{\mathrm{KL}}(p_{f},p_{g})\leq 2\varepsilon=2\|f-g\|_{\infty}. (161)

Mapping from ARM to EBM.

Given a context 𝒙∈𝒳{\bm{x}}\in{\mathcal{X}}, the probability according to an ARM of a response 𝒚=(y1,…,yτ)∈𝒴{\bm{y}}=(y_{1},\ldots,y_{\tau})\in{\mathcal{Y}}, with yτ=EOSy_{\tau}=\texttt{EOS}, decomposes as

pqarm​(𝒚|𝒙)\displaystyle p^{\textsc{arm}}_{q}({\bm{y}}|{\bm{x}}) =πq​(y1|𝒔1)​πq​(y2|𝒔2)​…​πq​(yτ|𝒔τ).\displaystyle=\pi_{q}(y_{1}|{\bm{s}}_{1})\pi_{q}(y_{2}|{\bm{s}}_{2})\dots\pi_{q}(y_{\tau}|{\bm{s}}_{\tau}). (162)

𝒔t≔{𝒙if ​t=1𝒙⊕𝒚<tif ​t>1,{\bm{s}}_{t}\coloneqq\begin{cases}{\bm{x}}&\mbox{if }t=1\\ {\bm{x}}\oplus{\bm{y}}_{<t}&\mbox{if }t>1\end{cases}, (163)

the conditional probabilities πq\pi_{q} as

πq​(y1|𝒔1)\displaystyle\pi_{q}(y_{1}|{\bm{s}}_{1}) ≔exp⁡(q⁡(𝒔1,y1)−Vq​(𝒔1))\displaystyle\coloneqq\exp(q({\bm{s}}_{1},y_{1})-V_{q}({\bm{s}}_{1})) (164)

⋮\displaystyle~~\vdots (166)
πq​(EOS|𝒔τ)\displaystyle\pi_{q}(\texttt{EOS}|{\bm{s}}_{\tau}) ≔exp⁡(q⁡(𝒔τ,EOS)−Vq​(𝒔τ))\displaystyle\coloneqq\exp(q({\bm{s}}_{\tau},\texttt{EOS})-V_{q}({\bm{s}}_{\tau})) (167)

and the (local) log-partitions as

Vq(𝒔t)≔log∑yt∈𝒜expq(𝒔t,yt).V_{q}({\bm{s}}_{t})\coloneqq\log\sum_{y_{t}\in{\mathcal{A}}}\exp q({\bm{s}}_{t},y_{t}). (168)

pqarm​(𝒚|𝒙)\displaystyle p^{\textsc{arm}}_{q}({\bm{y}}|{\bm{x}}) =exp⁡(q⁡(𝒔1,y1)+q⁡(𝒔2,y2)+⋯+q⁡(𝒔τ,EOS)−Vq​(𝒔1)−Vq​(𝒔2)−⋯−Vq​(𝒔τ))\displaystyle=\exp(q({\bm{s}}_{1},y_{1})+q({\bm{s}}_{2},y_{2})+\dots+q({\bm{s}}_{\tau},\texttt{EOS})-V_{q}({\bm{s}}_{1})-V_{q}({\bm{s}}_{2})-\dots-V_{q}({\bm{s}}_{\tau})) (169)

=pRrebm​(𝒚|𝒙),\displaystyle=p^{\textsc{ebm}}_{R_{r}}({\bm{y}}|{\bm{x}}), (171)

where RrR_{r} is defined in (20) and where we defined

⋮\displaystyle~~\vdots (173)

Because we can always define rr from RR using

r⁡(𝒔t,yt)≔{0if​yt≠EOSR⁡(𝒙,𝒚)if​yt=EOS,r({\bm{s}}_{t},y_{t})\coloneqq\begin{cases}0&\mbox{if}~y_{t}\neq\texttt{EOS}\\ R({\bm{x}},{\bm{y}})&\mbox{if}~y_{t}=\texttt{EOS}\\ \end{cases}, (182)

=minr∈ℱ⁡(𝒮×𝒜)⁡𝔼(X,Y)∼ρ​[−log⁡pℳ⁡(r)arm​(Y|X)]\displaystyle=\min_{r\in{\mathcal{F}}({\mathcal{S}}\times{\mathcal{A}})}{\mathbb{E}}_{(X,Y)\sim\rho}\left[-\log p^{\textsc{arm}}_{{\mathcal{M}}(r)}(Y|X)\right] (185)
=minq∈ℱ⁡(𝒮×𝒜)⁡𝔼(X,Y)∼ρ​[−log⁡pqarm​(Y|X)]\displaystyle=\min_{q\in{\mathcal{F}}({\mathcal{S}}\times{\mathcal{A}})}{\mathbb{E}}_{(X,Y)\sim\rho}\left[-\log p^{\textsc{arm}}_{q}(Y|X)\right] (186)
=minq∈ℱ⁡(𝒮×𝒜)⁡𝔼(X,Y)∼ρ​[ℓqarm​(X,Y)].\displaystyle=\min_{q\in{\mathcal{F}}({\mathcal{S}}\times{\mathcal{A}})}{\mathbb{E}}_{(X,Y)\sim\rho}\left[\ell^{\textsc{arm}}_{q}(X,Y)\right]. (187)

B.4 Proof of KL bound (Proposition 4.2)

From Lemma B.1, for all 𝒔t∈𝒮{\bm{s}}_{t}\in{\mathcal{S}}, we have

KL(πq(⋅|𝒔t),πq⋆(⋅|𝒔t))≤2∥q⋆(𝒔t,⋅)−q(𝒔t,⋅)∥∞.{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{q}(\cdot|{\bm{s}}_{t}),\pi_{q^{\star}}(\cdot|{\bm{s}}_{t}))\leq 2\|q^{\star}({\bm{s}}_{t},\cdot)-q({\bm{s}}_{t},\cdot)\|_{\infty}. (188)

This bounds the token-level distribution error.

We then have, for all 𝒙∈𝒳{\bm{x}}\in{\mathcal{X}},

KL(pqarm(⋅|𝒙),pq⋆arm(⋅|𝒙))\displaystyle{\mathrm{KL}}(p^{\textsc{arm}}_{q}(\cdot|{\bm{x}}),p^{\textsc{arm}}_{q^{\star}}(\cdot|{\bm{x}})) =∑t=1T𝔼StKL(πq⋆(⋅|St),πq(⋅|St))\displaystyle=\sum_{t=1}^{T}{\mathbb{E}}_{S_{t}}{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{q^{\star}}(\cdot|S_{t}),\pi_{q}(\cdot|S_{t})) (189)
≤2​∑t=1T𝔼St​‖q⋆​(St,⋅)−q⁡(St,⋅)‖∞\displaystyle\leq 2\sum_{t=1}^{T}{\mathbb{E}}_{S_{t}}\|q^{\star}(S_{t},\cdot)-q(S_{t},\cdot)\|_{\infty} (190)
≤2​T​max𝒔∈𝒮⁡(𝒙)​‖q⋆​(𝒔,⋅)−q⁡(𝒔,⋅)‖∞,\displaystyle\leq 2T\max_{{\bm{s}}\in{\mathcal{S}}({\bm{x}})}\|q^{\star}({\bm{s}},\cdot)-q({\bm{s}},\cdot)\|_{\infty}, (191)

where StS_{t} above is defined by St≔𝒙⊕Y<tS_{t}\coloneqq{\bm{x}}\oplus Y_{<t}, where Y<t∼ARπq⋆(⋅|𝒙)Y_{<t}\overset{\text{AR}}{\sim}\pi_{q^{\star}}(\cdot|{\bm{x}}). See also Appendix A.4 for more details.

This bounds the sequence-level distribution error.

Finally, using Proposition 3.2, we obtain

KL(pqarm(⋅|𝒙),pRrebm(⋅|𝒙))\displaystyle{\mathrm{KL}}(p^{\textsc{arm}}_{q}(\cdot|{\bm{x}}),p^{\textsc{ebm}}_{R_{r}}(\cdot|{\bm{x}})) =KL(pℳ⁡(r)arm(⋅|𝒙),pqarm(⋅|𝒙))\displaystyle={\mathrm{KL}}(p^{\textsc{arm}}_{{\mathcal{M}}(r)}(\cdot|{\bm{x}}),p^{\textsc{arm}}_{q}(\cdot|{\bm{x}})) (192)
≤2​T​max𝒔∈𝒮​‖ℳ⁡(r)​(𝒔,⋅)−q⁡(𝒔,⋅)‖∞.\displaystyle\leq 2T\max_{{\bm{s}}\in{\mathcal{S}}}\|{\mathcal{M}}(r)({\bm{s}},\cdot)-q({\bm{s}},\cdot)\|_{\infty}. (193)

B.5 Proof that an ARM defines a valid probability distribution (Proposition A.1)

By definition of 𝒴{\mathcal{Y}}, we have

∑𝒚∈𝒴pqarm​(𝒚|𝒙)=∑t=1T∑𝒚<t∈𝒱t−1pqarm​(𝒚<t⊕EOS|𝒙)=∑t=1Tlt\sum_{{\bm{y}}\in{\mathcal{Y}}}p^{\textsc{arm}}_{q}({\bm{y}}|{\bm{x}})=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{{\bm{y}}_{<t}\in{\mathcal{V}}^{t-1}}p^{\textsc{arm}}_{q}({\bm{y}}_{<t}\oplus\texttt{EOS}|{\bm{x}})=\sum_{t=1}^{T}l_{t} (194)

where

can be interpreted as the probability that a response has length tt. We can decompose ltl_{t} for any 1≤t≤T1\leq t\leq T as follows

lt\displaystyle l_{t} =∑𝒚<t∈𝒱t−1[∏k=1t−1πq​(yk|𝒔k)]​πq​(EOS|𝒔t)\displaystyle=\sum_{{\bm{y}}_{<t}\in{\mathcal{V}}^{t-1}}\left[\prod_{k=1}^{t-1}\pi_{q}(y_{k}|{\bm{s}}_{k})\right]\pi_{q}(\texttt{EOS}|{\bm{s}}_{t}) (195)
=(i)∑𝒚<t∈𝒱t−1[∏k=1t−1πq​(yk|𝒔k)]​(1−∑yt∈𝒱πq​(yt|𝒔t))\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(i)}}{{=}}\sum_{{\bm{y}}_{<t}\in{\mathcal{V}}^{t-1}}\left[\prod_{k=1}^{t-1}\pi_{q}(y_{k}|{\bm{s}}_{k})\right]\left(1-\sum_{y_{t}\in{\mathcal{V}}}\pi_{q}(y_{t}|{\bm{s}}_{t})\right) (196)
=Mt−Mt+1,\displaystyle=M_{t}-M_{t+1}, (197)

where M1≔1M_{1}\coloneqq 1 and for t>1t>1,

Mt≔∑𝒚<t∈𝒱t−1∏k=1t−1πq​(yk|𝒔k)=∑𝒚<t∈𝒱t−1pqarm​(𝒚<t|𝒙)M_{t}\coloneqq\sum_{{\bm{y}}_{<t}\in{\mathcal{V}}^{t-1}}\prod_{k=1}^{t-1}\pi_{q}(y_{k}|{\bm{s}}_{k})=\sum_{{\bm{y}}_{<t}\in{\mathcal{V}}^{t-1}}p_{q}^{\textsc{arm}}({\bm{y}}_{<t}|{\bm{x}})

In the derivations above, the equality in (i)(i) stems from the definition of the conditional probabilities through a softargmax{\operatorname{softargmax}}. By assumption, πq​(EOS|𝒔T)=1\pi_{q}(\texttt{EOS}|{\bm{s}}_{T})=1, which implies πq​(yT|𝒔T)=0\pi_{q}(y_{T}|{\bm{s}}_{T})=0 for any yT∈𝒱y_{T}\in{\mathcal{V}}. Consequently, no mass can continue beyond TT, therefore MT+1=0M_{T+1}=0 and we have shown the claim.

Appendix C Details on numerical illustrations

C.1 Setup

Architecture.

Both EBMs and ARMs use as a backbone a pre-layer norm Transformer with a scaled dot-product multihead attention, a positional embedder and a ReLU activation. We introduce the following notation:

  • •

    Size of the vocabulary: VV,

  • •

    Length of the sequences: TT,

  • •

    Number of blocks: NN,

  • •

    Embedding dimension: DD,

  • •

    Number of heads in the attention layer: HH,

  • •

    Hidden dimension in the MLP: FF.

The backbone Transformer is summarized below in abbreviated Flax code (Heek et al., 2024). It takes a sequence x_T∈𝒱T\in{\mathcal{V}}^{T} and outputs a representation x_TxD∈(ℝV)T\in({\mathbb{R}}^{V})^{T}.

⬇
class TransformerBlock(H, D, F):
def __call__(x_TxD, mask):
y_TxD = LayerNorm()(x_TxD)
y_TxD = MultiHeadAttention(H, D)(y_TxD, mask)
x_TxD = y_TxD + x_TxD
y_TxD = LayerNorm()(x_TxD)
y_TxF = Linear(F)(y_TxV)
y_TxF = relu(y_TxF)
y_TxD = Linear(D)(y_TxF)
x_TxD = y_TxD + x_TxD
return x_TxD
class Transformer(V, T, N, H, D, F):
def __call__(x_T, mask):
x_TxD = Embedder(V, D)(x_T)
y_TxD = Embedder(T, D)([0, ...,L])
x_TxD = x_TxD + y_TxD
for i in range(N):
TransformerBlock(H, D, F)(x_TxD, mask)
return x_TxD

For the ARM, the autoregressive dependency pattern is encoded through a mask applied to the attention matrix. The EBM does not use any mask. The ARM projects the embedded tokens into a space of size VV to define one logit per token. The EBM takes the average representation of the sequence along the sequence indexes and applies a final layer on the DD dimensional representation of the whole sequence to get a single score.

⬇
class AutoRegressiveModel((V, T, N, H, D F):
def __call__(x_T):
mask = make_causal_mask(x)
x_TxD = Transformer(V, T, N, H, D, F)(x_TxD, mask)
x_TxV = Linear(V)(x_TxD)
return x_TxV
class EnergyBasedModel(V, T, N, H, D, F):
def __call__(x_T):
x_TxD = Transformer(V, T, N, H, D, F)(x_TxD, None)
x_D = mean(x_TxD, axis=0)
x = Linear(1)(x_D)
return x

All sequences start with a BOS index. The BOS index is part of the embedder vocabulary but not part of the head (last linear transformation) of the ARM, since sentences can only end and not start again.

Objective function.

We compute the exact expected risk (39) and (40) by summing over all possible sequences and parameterizing the data distribution with a probability mass function ρ\rho of our choice. For simplicity, we use a fixed length TT. Concretely, using the EBM as an example, we compute the logits R⁡(𝒙,𝒚)R({\bm{x}},{\bm{y}}) for all possible sequences (𝒙,𝒚)({\bm{x}},{\bm{y}}) of length TT and then compute the loss using

ℒebm​(R)=∑(𝒙,𝒚)∈𝒱Tρ⁡(𝒙,𝒚)​ℓRebm​(𝒙,𝒚).{\mathcal{L}}^{{\textsc{ebm}}}(R)=\sum_{({\bm{x}},{\bm{y}})\in{\mathcal{V}}^{T}}\rho({\bm{x}},{\bm{y}})\ell_{R}^{{\textsc{ebm}}}({\bm{x}},{\bm{y}}).

For the data distribution ρ\rho, we tried two settings.

  1. 1.

    A Zipfian distribution over the set of all VTV^{T} sequences. This gives a distribution over all possible sequences with a large tail.

  2. 2.

    A normal-softargmax distribution, i.e., ρ=softargmax⁡(z/t)\rho={\operatorname{softargmax}}(z/t) for z∼𝒩⁡(0,1)z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1) a random normal vector, and t>0t>0 a temperature parameter. For small tt, this gives a vector of probability close to a one-hot vector among all possible sequences.

We briefly mentioned in the main text that ℒ⋆=−𝔼(X,Y)∼ρ​log⁡ρ⁡(𝒙,𝒚){\mathcal{L}}^{\star}=-{\mathbb{E}}_{(X,Y)\sim\rho}\log\rho({\bm{x}},{\bm{y}}) was the minimum of ℒebm​(R){\mathcal{L}}^{\textsc{ebm}}(R). To verify this, it suffices to observe that

ℒebm​(R)−ℒ⋆=KL⁡(ρ,softargmax⁡(R))≥0.{\mathcal{L}}^{{\textsc{ebm}}}(R)-{\mathcal{L}}^{\star}={\mathrm{KL}}(\rho,{\operatorname{softargmax}}(R))\geq 0.

Optimization.

We use the Adam optimizer (Kingma & Ba, 2014) with a trapezoidal schedule (warm-up of 100100 steps, constant learning rate η\eta, decay of 100 steps) with a learning rate η\eta searched in [3⋅10−3,1⋅10−3,10−4][3\cdot 10^{-3},1\cdot 10^{-3},10^{-4}]. We observed that the best learning rate (measured in terms of minimal area under the training curve) for EBMs matched the best learning rate for ARMs. Therefore, in the plots below, we simply choose the best learning rate for the EBM and use the same for the ARM.

C.2 Configurations.

We consider the following sequence spaces.

  1. 1.

    V=8,T=4V=8,T=4, leading to 4 0964\,096 sequences.

  2. 2.

    V=4,T=8V=4,T=8, leading to 65 53665\,536 sequences.

For these sequence spaces, we consider the following architectures

  1. 1.

    22-layer Transformer with N=2,H=2,D=16,V=16N=2,H=2,D=16,V=16. For V=8,T=4V=8,T=4 or V=4,T=8V=4,T=8, leading to to 3 6333\,633 parameters.

  2. 2.

    33-layer Transformer with N=3,H=4,D=64,F=64N=3,H=4,D=64,F=64. For V=8,T=4V=8,T=4 or V=4,T=8V=4,T=8, leading to 76 60976\,609 parameters.

The 22-layer Transformer is under-parameterized for V=8,T=4V=8,T=4 and V=4,T=8V=4,T=8, while the 33-layer Transformer is over-parameterized in those cases.

C.3 Metrics illustrated

To illustrate Proposition 4.1, we plot the losses along the training of these Transformers. Namely, in the left panel of Figures 2, 3 and 4, we plot

ℒebm​(R⁡(wk))−ℒ⋆,andℒarm​(q⁡(wk))−ℒ⋆,{\mathcal{L}}^{\textsc{ebm}}(R(w_{k}))-{\mathcal{L}}^{\star},\quad\text{and}\quad{\mathcal{L}}^{\textsc{arm}}(q(w_{k}))-{\mathcal{L}}^{\star},

where wkarmw_{k}^{\textsc{arm}} and wkebmw_{k}^{\textsc{ebm}} are the weights of, respectively, the ARM and EBM, at iteration kk of the training.

To illustrate our bijection result, after having optimized the EBM, we save the corresponding logits R⋆​(𝒙,𝒚)R^{\star}({\bm{x}},{\bm{y}}), and we then compare the logits qk​(𝒙,𝒚)q_{k}({\bm{x}},{\bm{y}}) of the ARM at iteration kk of its training, against the optimal EBM logits. We perform two comparisons.

The first one consists in simply summing the logits of the ARM along the sequence to get a scalar q¯k​(𝒙,𝒚)=∑t=1Tqk​(𝒔t,yt)\bar{q}_{k}({\bm{x}},{\bm{y}})=\sum_{t=1}^{T}q_{k}({\bm{s}}_{t},y_{t}) with 𝒔0=𝒙=BOS{\bm{s}}_{0}={\bm{x}}=\texttt{BOS} in our case, and 𝒔t,yt{\bm{s}}_{t},y_{t} defined as in the main text. This comparison amounts to think of the logits of the ARM as a score in itself like in the definition of the EBM model. We then center the scores of both the ARM and the EBM model (i.e., substract the mean score among all possible sequences), and measure the maximal absolute difference between them. Formally, we plot

‖c⁡(q¯k)−c⁡(R⋆)‖∞,\|c(\bar{q}_{k})-c(R^{\star})\|_{\infty},

where c⁡(𝒛)=𝒛−⟨𝒛,𝟏⟩​𝟏c({\bm{z}})={\bm{z}}-\langle{\bm{z}},{\mathbf{1}}\rangle{\mathbf{1}}. In Figures 2, 3 and 4, we call this measurement of the logits distance “Before mapping”.

The second comparison consists in computing q⋆=ℳ⁡(r⋆)q^{\star}={\mathcal{M}}(r^{\star}) for

r⋆​(𝒔t,yt)={0if​yt≠EOSR⋆​(𝒙,𝒚)if​yt=EOS.r^{\star}({\bm{s}}_{t},y_{t})=\begin{cases}0&\ \text{if}\ y_{t}\neq\texttt{EOS}\\ R^{\star}({\bm{x}},{\bm{y}})&\ \text{if}\ y_{t}=\texttt{EOS}\end{cases}.

This amounts to computing the ARM logits corresponding to the optimal EBM model via the mapping ℳ{\mathcal{M}} used in Proposition 3.2. We then center along the last axis the logits of the ARM at iteration kk and the logits of the EBM mapped in AR form. Finally, we plot their maximal absolute elementwise distance, i.e., we plot

‖c−1​(qk)−c−1​(ℳ⁡(r⋆))‖∞,\|c_{-1}(q_{k})-c_{-1}({\mathcal{M}}(r^{\star}))\|_{\infty},

where c−1c_{-1} denotes centering along the last axis. In Figures 2, 3 and 4, we call this measurement the logits distance “After mapping”.

In both cases, the centering is necessary to take care of the fact that, up to a constant factor, logits may define the same probability distribution through the softargmax{\operatorname{softargmax}} operator (Blondel & Roulet, 2024, Remark 4.2). Centering lets us discover, whether, up to some constant factor, the logits of the ARM converge to the logits predetermined by the EBM after an appropriate mapping.

C.4 Convergence and logits distance comparisons

Figure 2 illustrates the metrics explained above in the case V=8V=8, T=4T=4, for the 22-layer Transformer presented above.

We present some additional results here.

  • •

    In Figure 3, we vary the size of the Transformer and observe the same conclusions as in the main text.

  • •

    In Figure 4, we also try the case T>VT>V, namely, T=8,V=4T=8,V=4: same conclusions apply as in the main text.

The convergence in logits is challenged when using a different data distribution as explained in the next paragraph.

C.5 Bounding KL divergence by logits distance

In Figure 5, we compare KL divergence and distance between logits in infinity norm. Namely, as in the previous experiments, we compute the optimal logits for the EBM and then compare the logits of the ARM with the logits of the EBM mapped into ARM form. We use either the maximal absolute distance between logits, or we compare the KL distance between the probability distributions that the EBM and ARM define. We consider several setups (V>TV>T, T<VT<V, N=2N=2 or 33) with different definitions of the target distribution ρ\rho.

Proposition 4.2 stated that the KL should be upper bounded by the maximal absolute distance between logits. This is empirically confirmed in Figure 5.

Note that when we define the target distribution as a softargmax{\operatorname{softargmax}} of a normal vector (bottom panels in Figure 5), only the KL converges to 0, not the distance in infinity norm. In this case, the target distribution is extremely peaked towards a single sequence. So even if the distributions match after mapping the logits to the same vertex in the simplex of all sequences, the logits themselves may be far from each other. Another way to see that, is that the inverse mapping of the softargmax{\operatorname{softargmax}} is not Lipschitz continuous around a vertex of the simplex.

C.6 Optimization dynamics

Effect of learning rate.

In the previous experiments, we reported the results with the best learning rate. In Figure 6 and Figure 7, we compare EBMs and ARMs across different learning rates. In this experiment, both EBMs and ARMs achieve optimal performance at the same learning rate but ARMs are slightly more robust to learning rate specification.

Gradient noise analysis.

In Figure 8, we analyzed gradient noise using three metrics: gradient noise scale (GNS), gradient coherence and coordinate-wise signal-to-noise (SNR) ratio (see caption for their definitions. In this experiment, EBMs and ARMs are similarly sensitive to noise. This confirms once again one of the main messages of our paper: ARMs have the ability to behave very similarly to EBMs (while being much easier to train and sample from).
